**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 53, verses 1–3:**

﴿By the star when it sets,﴾ ﴿your companion has neither strayed nor erred,﴾ ﴿nor does he speak from desire.﴾ This is an address from God Most High to the polytheists who denigrated the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) concerning his prophethood.

Al-najm (the star): the heavenly body (al-kawkab), that is, the celestial body that appears to observers as shining in the atmosphere of the sky at night.

God Most High swore by one of His great creations, which points to the greatness of God's attributes.

The definite article in al-najm (the star) may be generic (li-l-jins), as in His words ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ [An-Nahl: 16] and His words ﴿and the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 6]. It may also be the definite article of previous reference (ta'rif al-'ahd). The most famous of the stars, when the word "the star" is used absolutely, is al-Thurayya (the Pleiades), because they used the times of its rising to mark the seasons and the ripening of fruits. Among their sayings is: "The star rose at evening, so the herdsman sought a cloak; the star rose at dawn, and the herdsman sought a waterskin (shukayya)." Shukayya is the diminutive of shakwa, a container made of leather in which water and milk are placed. They meant the beginning of the cold season and the beginning of the hot season.

It was also said that al-najm refers to al-Shi'ra al-Yamaniyya (Sirius), which is al-'Ubur, and it was held in high regard by the Arabs; the tribe of Khuza'a worshipped it.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of al-najm is the meteor (al-shihab), and its falling (hawy) is its descent from its place to another place. God said: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars﴾ [As-Saffat: 6] ﴿and as protection from every rebellious devil﴾ [As-Saffat: 7].

Page 90

And He said: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [Al-Mulk: 5].

The oath "﴿the piercing star﴾ [At-Tariq: 3]" is for what is in its creation of indication of the greatness of God's power. Do you not see God's saying, relating from Abraham: ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said, "This is my Lord"﴾ [Al-An'am: 76].

Restricting the oath by the star to the time of its setting indicates that the setting of this great creation comes after it has reached the height of its elevation on the horizon, which shows that it is subjected to God's power. For this reason Abraham said: ﴿I do not like those that set﴾ [Al-An'am: 76].

It is preferable that ﴿when it sets﴾ be a substitutive of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the star," because what is intended by "the star" is its conditions, which indicate the power of its Creator and Director. Among its greatest conditions is the state of its setting (hawy). Here idha (when) is a noun of time, stripped of the meaning of adverbial location, in a position of genitive governed by the particle of oath. By this we avoid the problem of seeking the complement of idha, a problem raised by the scholar al-Janzi against al-Zamakhshari. Al-Tibi said: In al-Muqtabas, al-Janzi said: "I discussed with Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) His words, Most High, ﴿By the star when it sets﴾: what governs idha? He said: What governs it is what the waw is attached to. I said: How can the verb of the present state govern the future, when its meaning is 'I swear now,' and its meaning is not 'I swear after this'? He then retracted and said: What governs it is a deleted verbal noun (masdar), its estimated form being: 'And the setting of the star when it sets.' I presented it to Zayn al-Mashaykh, and he did not approve of his second statement." The correct view is that idha has lost the meaning of futurity and has become for bare time. Its parallel is: "I will come to you when the unripe dates turn red," meaning at the time of their reddening; it has been stripped of the meaning of futurity, because the sufficiency was achieved by the words "I will come to you." End of al-Tibi's statement.

Page 91

Thus the correct view may be from the words of Zayn al-Mashaykh, or from the words of the author of al-Muqtabas, or from the words of al-Tibi. It is well-reasoned and is the basis upon which we have established the position of "idha" here. Al-Zamakhshari's hesitation regarding the answer was only because he holds that idha must be an adverb of the future, as is implied by his statements in al-Mufassal. Yet its departure from that meaning is agreed upon by the words of the verifying scholars.

Al-Huwiyy: falling (al-suqut). It is used here for the setting of the star, the falling being borrowed for its approach to disappearance. It is also permissible that al-huwiyy means the falling of a meteor when it appears to the observer that it is running across the face of the sky. In that case it is a literal falling, so the word is used in both its literal and figurative senses.

Mentioning ﴿when it sets﴾ is a safeguard against the polytheists supposing that the oath by the star is an affirmation of the worship of the star Sirius, and that swearing by it is an acknowledgment that it is a god, since some tribes of the Arabs worshipped it. The state of setting, expressed by hawy, is a state of descent and disappearance in the imagination of the observer, since they regard the rising of the star as its zenith of honour and regard its setting as its lowest point. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿So when it set, he said: I do not like those that set﴾ [Al-An'am: 76].

From the connections of this is His saying in this surah: ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [An-Najm: 49]. These are imaginative considerations common among them. It is beneficial to admonish people with this, because it is sufficient for convincing them and reaching the truth.

Thus His saying ﴿when it sets﴾ is an indication that all the stars are subjected to God's power, moving in their course within an order that He established for them, having no choice of their own, so they are not worthy of being worshipped. The purpose of the oath by what they contain of indication of divine power is thereby achieved, together with the safeguard against believing in their worship.

Al-Raghib said: It was said that by this (i.e., the star) He meant the Qur'an, revealed in installments, portion after portion, and by His saying "hawa" (fell) He meant its descent. End.

The connection of the oath "by the star when it sets" is that the discourse is directed toward establishing that the Qur'an is revelation from God, sent down from heaven. Thus the state of its descent in the metaphorical sense resembles the state of the star at its setting, a figurative resemblance arising from the descent of a luminous thing giving a spiritual illumination, descending from a place of spiritual elevation.

Page 92

It is likened to the state of a star descending from the highest part of the horizon to its lowest. This is the representation of the intelligible by the perceptible. Or it refers to the resemblance between the state of Gabriel's descent from the heavens and the state of a star descending from its highest place to its lowest. Or it is the likening of a perceptible thing to a perceptible thing, as with the falling of a meteor. People sometimes liken the speed of running to the falling of a meteor. Aws ibn Hajr said, describing a horse:

*"He dashed like a shooting star, followed by dust that rises, you think it is the tent-rope."*

Al-dalal (going astray): failing to find the path that leads to the intended goal. It is a metaphor for following what contradicts the truth.

Al-ghiwaya (error): corruption of opinion and attachment to falsehood.

Al-sahib (companion): the one who is constantly with the person to whom the description "companion" is attached. The intended meaning of "companion" here is one who has dealings and conditions in relation to the one attached to him, and the intended one is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is like the saying of Abu Ma'bad al-Khuza'i, recorded in the course of the story of the Hijra, when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered his tent, in which was Umm Ma'bad, who related to him the miracle of his wiping the udder of her goat: "This is the companion of Quraysh," meaning the companion of the events that occurred between him and them.

Expressing him by the description "your companion" is a veiled reproach that they are people of slander, since they attributed to him what has nothing to do with him, despite their intense knowledge of his conditions and affairs, for he was among them in a town where it is not difficult for the people to know the condition of a specific individual who was among them. In the sermon of al-Hajjaj after the battle of Dayr al-Jamajim, he said to the Kharijites: "Were you not my companions in al-Ahwaz, when you planned treachery and concealed disbelief?" He meant that their conditions were not hidden from him, so they could not attempt to disown their sins through deception and doubt.

This is a rebuttal from God to the polytheists and an invalidation of their statements about the Prophet (ﷺ), since they said: "He is possessed," and they said: "He is a poet," and they said about the Qur'an: "This is nothing but fabrication."

Madness is among the forms of going astray, since the madman cannot find the means of right conduct; and lying and sorcery are straying and error.

Page 93

Poetry as commonly known among them is error, as God Most High said: ﴿And the poets, those astray follow them﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 224], meaning that they favour their statements because they are error.

Joined to the answer of the oath is ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾. This is a description of perfection of his essence. The discourse that he utters is the Qur'an, because they said about it: ﴿This is nothing but a lie that he has invented﴾ [Al-Furqan: 4], and they said: ﴿Legends of the former peoples that he has had written down﴾ [Al-Furqan: 5]. That, and the like of it, is nothing but his invention or choice out of love for what he invents and chooses, regardless of whether it is true or false. For poetry contains wisdom, and it contains narration of events, and it contains imaginings and fabrications. All of it arises from the poet's love for saying such things. So God showed them that the Qur'an calls to good.

The particle "ma" is negating: it negated that he speaks from desire.

Al-hawa (desire): the inclination of the soul toward what it loves or wishes to do, without this being required by sound and wise reason. For this reason people differ in their desires and do not differ regarding the truth. A person may love the truth and what is right, so when desire is mentioned without qualification, the intended meaning is desire stripped of evidence.

The negation of speaking from desire requires the negation of the whole category of what he says from being characterised as issuing from desire, whether it is the Qur'an or other prophetic guidance, such as teaching, exhortation, admonition and wisdom. But the Qur'an is the principal intended meaning, because it is the cause of this rebuttal against them.

Know that the declaration that he (ﷺ) is free from speaking from desire requires his freedom from acting or judging from desire, because freedom from speaking from desire is the highest rank of wisdom. For this reason it is reported in the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would joke but would say nothing except the truth. Here the refutation of their statement is complete, so it is fitting to pause at His saying ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾.

Between (hawa, "fell") and (al-hawa, "desire") there is a near-perfect paronomasia (jinas shibh al-tamm).

Or it refers to the resemblance between the state of Gabriel's descent from the heavens and the state of a star descending from its highest place to its lowest. Or it is the likening of a perceptible thing to a perceptible thing, as with the falling of a meteor. People sometimes liken the speed of running to the falling of a meteor. Aws ibn Hajr said, describing a horse:

*"He dashed like a shooting star, followed by dust that rises, you think it is the tent-rope."*

Al-dalal (going astray): failing to find the path that leads to the intended goal. It is a metaphor for following what contradicts the truth.

Al-ghiwaya (error): corruption of opinion and attachment to falsehood.

Al-sahib (companion): the one who is constantly with the person to whom the description "companion" is attached. The intended meaning of "companion" here is one who has dealings and conditions in relation to the one attached to him, and the intended one is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is like the saying of Abu Ma'bad al-Khuza'i, recorded in the course of the story of the Hijra, when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered his tent, in which was Umm Ma'bad, who related to him the miracle of his wiping the udder of her goat: "This is the companion of Quraysh," meaning the companion of the events that occurred between him and them.

Expressing him by the description "your companion" is a veiled reproach that they are people of slander, since they attributed to him what has nothing to do with him, despite their intense knowledge of his conditions and affairs, for he was among them in a town where it is not difficult for the people to know the condition of a specific individual who was among them. In the sermon of al-Hajjaj after the battle of Dayr al-Jamajim, he said to the Kharijites: "Were you not my companions in al-Ahwaz, when you planned treachery and concealed disbelief?" He meant that their conditions were not hidden from him, so they could not attempt to disown their sins through deception and doubt.

This is a rebuttal from God to the polytheists and an invalidation of their statements about the Prophet (ﷺ), since they said: "He is possessed," and they said: "He is a poet," and they said about the Qur'an: "This is nothing but fabrication."

Madness is among the forms of going astray, since the madman cannot find the means of right conduct; and lying and sorcery are straying and error.

Page 93

Poetry as commonly known among them is error, as God Most High said: ﴿And the poets, those astray follow them﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 224], meaning that they favour their statements because they are error.

Joined to the answer of the oath is ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾. This is a description of perfection of his essence. The discourse that he utters is the Qur'an, because they said about it: ﴿This is nothing but a lie that he has invented﴾ [Al-Furqan: 4], and they said: ﴿Legends of the former peoples that he has had written down﴾ [Al-Furqan: 5]. That, and the like of it, is nothing but his invention or choice out of love for what he invents and chooses, regardless of whether it is true or false. For poetry contains wisdom, and it contains narration of events, and it contains imaginings and fabrications. All of it arises from the poet's love for saying such things. So God showed them that the Qur'an calls to good.

The particle "ma" is negating: it negated that he speaks from desire.

Al-hawa (desire): the inclination of the soul toward what it loves or wishes to do, without this being required by sound and wise reason. For this reason people differ in their desires and do not differ regarding the truth. A person may love the truth and what is right, so when desire is mentioned without qualification, the intended meaning is desire stripped of evidence.

The negation of speaking from desire requires the negation of the whole category of what he says from being characterised as issuing from desire, whether it is the Qur'an or other prophetic guidance, such as teaching, exhortation, admonition and wisdom. But the Qur'an is the principal intended meaning, because it is the cause of this rebuttal against them.

Know that the declaration that he (ﷺ) is free from speaking from desire requires his freedom from acting or judging from desire, because freedom from speaking from desire is the highest rank of wisdom. For this reason it is reported in the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would joke but would say nothing except the truth. Here the refutation of their statement is complete, so it is fitting to pause at His saying ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾.

Between (hawa, "fell") and (al-hawa, "desire") there is a near-perfect paronomasia (jinas shibh al-tamm).

﴿It is nothing but a revelation revealed.﴾ ﴿One mighty in power taught him,﴾ ﴿endowed with strength, and he stood firm,﴾ ﴿while he was on the highest horizon.﴾ ﴿Then he drew near and came down,﴾ ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer.﴾ ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (istinaf bayani) following the phrase ﴿And he does not speak from desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3].

The pronoun in "huwa" refers to the thing spoken, derived from the verb "yanṭiqu" (he speaks), as in His saying ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], meaning: the justice derived from the verb ﴿Be just﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8].

It is also possible that the pronoun refers to something understood from the context of the refutation directed at them, since in their statements refuted by His saying ﴿Your companion has not gone astray, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2], they claimed that the Qur'an was sorcery, or poetry, or soothsaying, or the fables of the ancients, or a fabrication he had invented.

Even if the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke other than the Qur'an by revelation, as in the hadith of al-Hudaybiyah, in his answer to the one who asked him: "And what does the one performing 'umrah do?", and as in his saying: "Indeed the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has completed its appointed term," and like all the sacred hadith (ahadith qudsiyyah) in which he says, "God Most High said," and the like.

The phrase "yuha" (is revealed) emphasizes the phrase ﴿it is nothing but a revelation﴾, together with the indication of the present tense that what he speaks is a continuously renewed revelation that does not cease.

The complement of "yuha" is omitted, its estimated form being "ilayhi" (to him), that is, to your companion.

The agent of the revelation is omitted for a kind of generality that is followed by detail, because after it there will come what explains it, namely His saying ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.﴾

The clause ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ and what follows is a resumptive explanatory clause, explaining how the revelation took place.

The pronoun of the absent in "ʿallamahu" refers to the revelation, or to what the pronoun "huwa" in His saying ﴿it is nothing but a revelation﴾ refers to. The pronoun "huwa" refers to the Qur'an. It is in the position of one of the two objects of "ʿallama" (to teach), the first object, and the second object is omitted, the estimated form being "ʿallamahu iyyahu" (taught him it), referring to your companion. It is also permissible to make the pronoun "hu" in "ʿallamahu" refer to your companion and the omitted object refer to revelation, as a refutation of the claim of the polytheists: ﴿It is only a human who teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103].

Here "ʿallama" is transitive to two objects, because it is the doubled form of "ʿalima" which is transitive to one object.

The phrase ﴿One mighty in power﴾ is an attribute of an omitted noun indicated by what is mentioned afterward of the matters belonging to the angels, meaning: an angel mighty in power. The commentators agreed that what is meant by it is Gabriel (Jibril), peace be upon him.

What is meant by "al-quwa" (power) is the capacity to carry out what God commands of great deeds, both intellectual and physical. He is the angel who descends upon the messengers with the conveyance (of the message).

"Al-mirrah" (strength) — with a kasra on the mim and a shadda on the ra' with a fatha — is used for the strength of the essence and is also used for the solidity and originality of the intellect, and this is what is meant here, because before it there has already been the description "mighty in power." The singling out of Gabriel with this attribute indicates that he is the angel who descends with the outpourings of wisdom upon

[Page 96]

the messengers and prophets. For this reason, when the angel offered the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the Isra' a cup of milk and a cup of wine, and he chose the milk, Gabriel said to him: "You have chosen the natural disposition (fitrah). Had you taken the wine, your community would have gone astray."

His saying "fastawa" (and he stood firm) is a branch (consequence) of what preceded it, His saying ﴿taught him, one mighty in power﴾.

The fa' is for the detail of "ʿallamahu", and the one who stood firm is Gabriel. The meaning of his standing firm is his rising with resolve to receive the message of God, as one says "istaqalla qa'iman" (he stood up erect) and as one says "bayna yadayi fulan" (in front of so-and-so). So Gabriel's standing firm is the beginning of readiness to accept the message from God. For this reason this standing firm is restricted by the circumstantial clause in His saying ﴿while he was on the highest horizon.﴾ The pronoun refers to Gabriel without doubt, that is, before he descended to the earthly world.

"Al-ufuq" (horizon) is a name for the atmosphere that appears to the observer as the meeting point between the extremity of the sight's limit from the earth and the limit of what appears like a blue dome. Its use became dominant for a distant region away from the location of the people, and from it come "the horizon of the east" and "the horizon of the west."

Its description as "al-a'la" (highest) in this verse indicates that it is a region of the atmosphere of the sky. This was mentioned so that His saying ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ might be built upon it.

The "thumma" (then) is coordinating with the clause "fastawa," and the delay indicated by "thumma" is a delay of rank, because drawing near to where the revelation reaches is the more important matter in this context.

"Al-dunuww" means nearness. Since the verb of drawing near has been joined by "thumma" to "istawa bi'l-ufuq al-a'la" (stood firm on the highest horizon), it is known that he drew near to the earthly world, that is, he began to draw near after receiving what he conveys to the Messenger (ﷺ).

"Tadalla" means he descended from a height a little, that is, he comes down from levels to what is beneath them, as a suspended object in the air hangs down, such that if an observer saw it he would think it hanging, while in fact it descends from the sky without swooping down.

As for "qab" (in "qāba qawsayn"), it was said its meaning is "measure." It is a word with a waw as its middle radical, and it is said "qab" and "qib" with a kasra on the qaf, and this is what most of the commentators followed. It was also said that "qab" is used for what lies between the grip of the bow, that is, the middle of its curved wood, and what lies between its two "siyat" (tips), that is, its two ends that bend and to which the string is tied. So the bow has two "qabs" and two "siyat," and perhaps this usage is the original for the other. On this meaning al-Farra', al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn 'Atiyyah interpreted it, and from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: "al-qab" is the front of the Arab bow, where the strap is tied, which its owner holds, and every bow has one qab.

On both interpretations, His saying ﴿qāba qawsayn﴾ originally is "qābay qaws" or "qābay qawsayn" (by making dual one of the two words, the construct or the genitive, or both), so the singular of one of the two words or both was used to avoid the heaviness of the dual, as in His saying ﴿If you two repent to God, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], meaning: "qalbakuma" (your two hearts).

It was also said that in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz "qaws" is used for a cubit by which something is measured (perhaps then it is the verbal noun of "qasa," so what is measured by it is named after it).

The "qaws" (bow) is an instrument of yew wood, curved, to which a string of leather is attached and from which arrows are shot, and the "nushab" (arrow); and it is about the length of a cubit among the Arabs.

The summary of the meaning is that Gabriel was at a distance of two bow-lengths from the Prophet (ﷺ), indicated by the consequential clause in His saying ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.﴾ Perhaps the wisdom in this distance is that this description is an depiction of the form of revelation that was at the beginning of the Prophet's time of prophethood, when his human powers were not accustomed to bearing the direct contact of the angelic power, out of kindness to the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he would not undertake anything that would be hard for him. Do you not see that when contact with him occurred in the cave of Hira', there was no contact? It is what he described in his hadith as "ghatt" (pressing), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He pressed me until I reached the limit of exertion." Then the state described in the hadith of the descent of the first revelation, referred to in Surah al-Muddaththir and Surah al-Muzzammil, would come upon him. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed We shall cast upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. Then he became accustomed to Gabriel's direct contact with him. It has been reported in the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning the question of Gabriel about faith, Islam, excellence (ihsan), and the Hour, that he sat before the Prophet (ﷺ) and placed his knees against the Prophet's knees, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was at that time in Madinah and had become accustomed to revelation, and its severity had left him.

For the sake of observing this wisdom, Gabriel would appear to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of a man. 'Umar described him in the hadith explaining faith and Islam, saying: "A man came in to us, extremely white of garments and extremely black of hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and none of us knew him..." (the hadith). And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them after he had left: "O 'Umar, do you know who the questioner was?" 'Umar said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "It was Gabriel. He came to you to teach you your religion."

His saying ﴿aw adna﴾ (or nearer): the "aw" here is for choice in estimation, and it is used for approximation, meaning: if anyone wishes to approximate this distance, he may choose between making it "two bow-lengths" or "nearer," that is, not more. It is an indication that the estimation is not an exaggeration.

The consequence of ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ upon His saying ﴿then he descended﴾ ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths﴾, which is a consequence of the consequence of His saying ﴿taught him, one mighty in power﴾, is what is intended by the explanation, and what precedes it is a preparation for it, and an illustration of wondrous states by means of what people most readily understand, for the purpose of explaining the possibility of receiving revelation from God Most High, since the polytheists were denying it. So He explained to them the possibility of revelation by describing the manner of revelation in general terms, and this is one form of the forms of revelation.

The choice of expressing the Prophet (ﷺ) by the title "His servant" is an explicit mention in place of the pronoun, to convey, through the idafa (attribution) to the divine name, the honour of distinction.

In His saying ﴿what He revealed﴾ there is an ambiguity intended to magnify what was revealed to him.

the messengers and prophets. On both interpretations, His saying ﴿qāba qawsayn﴾ originally is "qābay qaws" or "qābay qawsayn" (by making dual one of the two words, the construct or the genitive, or both), so the singular of one of the two words or both was used to avoid the heaviness of the dual, as in His saying ﴿If you two repent to God, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], meaning: "qalbakuma" (your two hearts).

It was also said that in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz "qaws" is used for a cubit by which something is measured (perhaps then it is the verbal noun of "qasa," so what is measured by it is named after it).

The "qaws" (bow) is an instrument of yew wood, curved, to which a string of leather is attached and from which arrows are shot, and the "nushab" (arrow); and it is about the length of a cubit among the Arabs.

The summary of the meaning is that Gabriel was at a distance of two bow-lengths from the Prophet (ﷺ), indicated by the consequential clause in His saying ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.﴾ Perhaps the wisdom in this distance is that this description is an depiction of the form of revelation that was at the beginning of the Prophet's time of prophethood, when his human powers were not accustomed to bearing the direct contact of the angelic power, out of kindness to the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he would not undertake anything that would be hard for him. Do you not see that when contact with him occurred in the cave of Hira', there was no contact? It is what he described in his hadith as "ghatt" (pressing), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He pressed me until I reached the limit of exertion." Then the state described in the hadith of the descent of the first revelation, referred to in Surah al-Muddaththir and Surah al-Muzzammil, would come upon him. God Most High said: ﴿Indeed We shall cast upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. Then he became accustomed to Gabriel's direct contact with him. It has been reported in the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning the question of Gabriel about faith, Islam, excellence (ihsan), and the Hour, that he sat before the Prophet (ﷺ) and placed his knees against the Prophet's knees, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was at that time in Madinah and had become accustomed to revelation, and its severity had left him.

[Page 98]

For the sake of observing this wisdom, Gabriel would appear to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of a man. 'Umar described him in the hadith explaining faith and Islam, saying: "A man came in to us, extremely white of garments and extremely black of hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and none of us knew him..." (the hadith). And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them after he had left: "O 'Umar, do you know who the questioner was?" 'Umar said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "It was Gabriel. He came to you to teach you your religion."

His saying ﴿aw adna﴾ (or nearer): the "aw" here is for choice in estimation, and it is used for approximation, meaning: if anyone wishes to approximate this distance, he may choose between making it "two bow-lengths" or "nearer," that is, not more. It is an indication that the estimation is not an exaggeration.

The consequence of ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ upon His saying ﴿then he descended﴾ ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths﴾, which is a consequence of the consequence of His saying ﴿taught him, one mighty in power﴾, is what is intended by the explanation, and what precedes it is a preparation for it, and an illustration of wondrous states by means of what people most readily understand, for the purpose of explaining the possibility of receiving revelation from God Most High, since the polytheists were denying it. So He explained to them the possibility of revelation by describing the manner of revelation in general terms, and this is one form of the forms of revelation.

The pronoun in "awha" refers to God Most High, known from His saying ﴿it is nothing but a revelation revealed﴾, as has been mentioned. The meaning: "So He revealed to His servant Muhammad (ﷺ) what He revealed."

This is sufficient in this context, because what is intended is establishing the act of revelation in refutation of their denial of it.

The choice of expressing the Prophet (ﷺ) by the title "His servant" is an explicit mention in place of the pronoun, to convey, through the idafa (attribution) to the divine name, the honour of distinction.

In His saying ﴿what He revealed﴾ there is an ambiguity intended to magnify what was revealed to him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 11–12:

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾

The more evident view is that this is a rebuttal of the denial by the polytheists of what had reached them of the report about the Prophet ﷺ seeing the angel Jibril, which is indicated by His saying after ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾.

[Page 99]

The lam in His saying ﴿al-fu'ad (the heart)﴾ is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: his heart. On this basis, the interrogative that follows in His saying ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ is a rhetorical interrogative of denial, because they had disputed with him.

It is also permissible that His saying ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ is an emphasis of the content of His saying ﴿and he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾ [al-Najm: 9], for it indicates that he was within the sight of the Prophet ﷺ, thereby removing the possibility of a metaphor in the comparison of nearness; that is, it is a sensory nearness and not merely a spiritual connection. Then the interrogative in His saying ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ is used in the sense of supposition and assumption, meaning: will you then deny him regarding what he sees with his own eyes, just as you denied him regarding what reached you from Allah? It is like one who says, "Do you think me heedless?" and like the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to al-'Abbas and 'Ali in their case: "Are you trying to get from me a judgment other than that?!"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿mā kadhaba﴾ with a light dhal, while Hisham from Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with a heavy dhal; the subject and object remain as they are in the reading of the majority.

Al-fu'ad (the heart): in the speech of the Arabs it means the intellect. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾ [al-Qasas: 10].

Al-kadhib (lying): it is applied to imagining and deceiving by the senses, as one says, "His eye deceived him" (kadhdhabat-hu 'aynuhu).

Ma is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun (the connecting element) is omitted; it is a pronoun referring to His servant in His saying ﴿Then He revealed to His servant﴾ [al-Najm: 10], meaning: what his servant saw with his sight.

The derivation of ﴿Will you then dispute﴾ is from the sentence ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

The majority read ﴿afa-tumāruna-hu﴾ from al-muma'ara, which is wrangling and disputing over invalidation. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (afa-tamrunahu) with a fatha on the taa' and a sukun on the miim, the imperfect of marahu when one denies it, meaning: will you also deny him regarding what he saw? The meanings of the two readings are close.

[Page 100]

The verb is made transitive in both readings by the preposition of elevation (ʿalā), because it includes the meaning of overpowering, meaning: suppose you have overpowered him in your worship of the gods and in turning away from hearing the Qur'an and the like; will you overpower him regarding what he saw with his eyes?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 13–18:

﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ ﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ ﴿near which is the Garden of Refuge﴾ ﴿when there covered the Lote-tree that which covers﴾ ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. That is: if you deny his being seen on earth, then he saw him with a vision greater than it, when he saw him in the higher world in company. This is among the ascending progression in explaining the stages of revelation, and the conjunction is the conjunction of one narrative upon another, beginning with the weaker and following with the stronger.

The emphasis of the speech with the oath-lam and the particle of confirmation is due to what is in this report of strangeness, in that he saw Jibril, and in that he was taken up to the heaven, and of importance, in that it indicates the great station of Muhammad ﷺ. The pronoun of the nominative in "raʼahu" refers to your companion, and the pronoun of the accusative refers to Jibril.

"Nazlatan" is on the pattern fa'lah from descent (nuzul), so it is a verbal noun indicating the single occurrence, that is: in another place of descent, which is alighting in a place. He described it as "ukhra" (another) in relation to what is in His saying ﴿Then he approached and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8], for descending (tadalli) is a descent to the place which he reached.

The accusative of "nazlatan" is either by removal of the preposition, or as a substitute for the adverb of place, or by omitting a modifier with the estimate: "at the time of another descent," so it is a substitute for the adverb of place.

His saying ﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ is connected to "raʼahu." The sight at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary was singled out for mention because of the great nobility of the place by what occurred there of the greatest signs of his Lord, and because it is the endpoint of ascent in the stages of honour.

"Sidrat al-Muntaha" is a name the Qur'an applied to a higher place above the seventh heaven, and its explicit mention has come in the sound reports of the Night Journey from a group of the Companions.

Perhaps that place was likened to the lote-tree, which is one tree of the lote (sidr) kind, either in the description of its branching, or in that it is a limit at which the nearness of the Prophet ﷺ ended, to a place which no angel had reached before him. Perhaps this is based on a convention among them of placing lote-trees at the boundaries of territories.

The idafa of "sidrah" to "al-Muntaha" may be an explanatory (bayaniyyah) idafa. It may also be for defining the lote-tree by a place where it ends, which no one passes beyond, because what lies beyond it is beyond the capacity of created beings.

"Sidrah" is the single form of "sidr," which is the jujube tree. They said it is distinguished by three qualities: long shade, pleasant taste, and fragrant scent, so the lote-tree was made a likeness of that place, just as the palm tree was made a likeness of the believer.

In His saying ﴿what covered it covered﴾ there is vagueness for general magnification, and that the expressions of description in the language are too narrow for it.

"Jannat al-Ma'wa" is the well-known Garden, described as the abode of the God-fearing, for the Garden is the endpoint of the stages of elevation of pure souls. In the report of the Night Journey, after mention of the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, there is: "Then I was made to enter the Garden."

His saying ﴿when there covered the Lote-tree that which covers﴾ is a stationary adverbial clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from ﴿Sidrat al-Muntaha﴾, intended to draw attention to the majesty and beauty that surrounded this place called Sidrat al-Muntaha. In the report of the Night Journey: "Until I arrived at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and there covered it colours I do not know what they are," and in another narration: "There covered it a light from Allah, which no one can look upon." As for what the Prophet ﷺ attained there of honour by receiving revelation directly from Allah without the intermediary of the angel, in the report of the Night Journey: "Until I reached a level where I heard the scratching of the pens, and Allah prescribed for my community fifty prayers," the hadith.

The clause ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ is a parenthetical clause, and it has the meaning of the clause ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ to its end, that is: he saw Jibril with a vision in which there is no error and no addition to what he described, that is, no exaggeration.

The swerving (zaygh) is inclining away from the intended course, that is, his sight did not incline to any other object seen besides what was mentioned, and transgression (tughyan) is going beyond the limit.

The clause ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil), that is: he saw signs other than the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, the Garden of Refuge, and what covered the Lote-tree of the splendour and majesty; he saw of the greatest signs of Allah.

The "signs" (ayat) are the evidences of the greatness of Allah, the Exalted, which increase the Messenger in elevation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 19–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza,﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ ﴿That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ ﴿They are but names you have named them, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

When the discussion had passed over the description of the revelation and the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) witnessing of Jibril (peace be upon him), and over what indicates the sublime matters of the greatness of Allah the Exalted and the nobility of His Messenger (ﷺ) and the nobility of Jibril (peace be upon him), in that he was described with attributes of perfection and stations of honour, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) was described with ascent through the exalted stations, this naturally evoked a comparison between these lofty states and the state of the greatest of their three gods, according to their claim, namely: al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat, which are stones whose place is the earth, having no power of disposal, and by which no one ascends to any height. Thus this opposition formed a comprehensive imaginary contrast which called for following the mention of those states with the mention of the states of these.

The discourse thus shifted from the purpose of establishing that the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed to with the Qur'an, to the refutation of idol worship. The basis of the refutation is His saying: ﴿They are but names you have named them, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The fa' (so) here is for the derivation of the interrogation and what follows it from the sentence ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12], which is derived from the sentence ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ [al-Najm: 11].

The seeing in "a-fa-ra'aytum" may be visual, transitive to one object, so it does not require a second object, and the interrogation is then one of affirmation with mockery, meaning: how do you see al-Lat
صفحة ١٠٣
and al-Uzza and Manat in relation to what has been described of the greatness of Allah the Exalted, and the nobility of His angels and the nobility of His Messenger (ﷺ)? This is mockery of them and a refutation of the divinity of those idols by way of implication, and its evidence is direct observation. The most common usage of ara'ayta is for visual seeing, according to what Radi al-Din chose.

The sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ etc. may be a resumption and an escalation in the refutation, or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the sentence ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza﴾, since its content is among what their claims include: they used to claim that al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat were the daughters of Allah, as Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Kashshaf have related from them, and the context of the verses requires it.

It is also possible that the seeing is cognitive, meaning: do you suppose al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat [to be so]? The second object is then omitted for brevity, the indication being His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ upon it. The estimate is: you supposed them to be daughters of Allah; do you attribute to Him the female while you seek male sons? The sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ then serves as an explanation of the denial and an escalation in refuting their claims, meaning: do you assign to Allah daughters exclusively, while you take pride in male sons for yourselves?

Sahib al-Kashf made His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ take the place of the second object of "ara'aytum".

Also, since what preceded of the description of revelation and the stations of nearness in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was honoured, and the greatness of Jibril, carried an indication of the vastness of the power of Allah the Exalted and the magnitude of His dominion, which records against the polytheists, in their claim, partners to Allah—idols such as al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat—the corruption of their claim and the foolishness of their opinion, there followed the mention of indications of divine greatness with the refutation of the divinity of their idols, in that they are lower than the rank of divinity, since those are illusions that have no realities, but were invented by the imaginings of the people of polytheism, who gave them names for which there are no realities. Thus He branched off with ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza?﴾ etc. The interrogation is then one of affirmation and denial, and the seeing is cognitive, and the second object is His saying ﴿They are but names you have named them﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The sentence ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ etc. may be parenthetical between the two objects, for escalation in denial, meaning: you supposed them to be daughters of Allah, or you supposed the angels to be daughters of Allah.
صفحة ١٠٤
These aspects are not mutually exclusive, so we take them to mean that all of them are intended in this context.

You may also make the verb "ara'aytum" (on the basis that the seeing is cognitive) suspended from operating, because the negating "in" follows it in His saying ﴿They are but names you have named them﴾ [al-Najm: 23], and make the sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ up to His saying "﴿unjust﴾" a parenthetical clause.

Al-Lat: an idol that belonged to the Thaqif at al-Ta'if, which Quraysh and the majority of the Arabs worshipped, and it had fame among Quraysh. It is a square rock on which they built a structure. Al-Razi said it was in the form of a man, and it was at the place of the left minaret of the mosque of al-Ta'if; so said al-Qurtubi. Perhaps the mosque had two minarets.

The alif and lam at the beginning of al-Lat are additional, and the "al" that enters upon it is additional, and perhaps that is because its origin is "Latt," meaning "a worshipped one." When they wished to make it a proper name for a specific worshipped one, they added to it the lam of definiteness of familiarity, as in Allah, whose origin is ilah. It is pausal with the sukun on its ta' in standard Arabic.

The majority read (al-Latta) with a light taa'. Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a doubled taa', and this is a dialect for this name, since many Arabs say: the origin of its rock is a place where a man used to sit in the Jahiliyya, kneading sawiq for the pilgrims; when he died they took his place as a shrine.

Al-Uzza: the form fu'la from al-'izz (might): the name of an idol of white stone with a structure over it. Al-Razi said it was in the form of a plant; perhaps he means that the rock had in it the form of a tree. It was in the hollow of a palm tree above Dhat 'Irq. The majority of the Arabs worshipped it, especially Quraysh, and Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud, addressing the Muslims: "We have al-Uzza and you have no Uzza."

Al-Zamakhshari, in his commentary on Surat al-Fatiha, mentioned that the Arabs, when they began an action, would say: "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-Uzza."

As for Manat, it is a proper noun that is original (martajal), and it is feminine, so the rule is that it be written with the feminine ha' at its end and be paused on with the ha', and it is non-declinable. There is also a dialect with the original taa' at its end, so it is paused on with the taa' and is declinable, because the taa' of Lat is like the ba' of Bab. Its origin is manwa, with a vowel, and it may be lengthened, so one says manaa'a. It is non-declinable for being a proper name and feminine. The analogical pausal form is with the ha', but some pause with the taa' following the script of the Mushaf. It was a rock, worshipped by the majority of the Arabs, and its place was at al-Mushallal, near Qudayd between Makkah and Madinah. The Aws and the Khazraj would circumambulate around it during the Hajj instead of al-Safa and al-Marwa. When the Muslims performed Hajj and ran between al-Safa and al-Marwa, the Ansar were reluctant to run because they used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwa; then there came down concerning them His saying ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah; so whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], as has preceded from the hadith of 'A'isha in the Muwatta' in Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority read "wa-Manat" with a taa' after the alif, and Ibn Kathir read it with a hamza after the alif, according to one of the two dialects. The majority pause on it with the taa', following the orthography of the Mushaf, so the taa' is a letter of the word and not a feminine marker; it is like the taa' of al-Lat, and they make its writing in the Mushaf contrary to analogy.

Its description as "the third" is because it is third in mention, and this is a clarifying attribute; its description as "the other" is also a clarifying attribute, because its being third in mention, after the two mentioned before it, is known to the hearer. The result of the two attributes is the emphasis of its mention. This is because al-Lat and al-Uzza are more famous among Quraysh and among the majority of the Arabs than Manat, owing to the distance of Manat's place from their lands; and because the arrangement of the locations of the houses of these idols is likewise: al-Lat is in the upper Tihama at al-Ta'if, al-Uzza is in its middle at Nakhla between Makkah and al-Ta'if, and Manat is at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah, so it is the third of the regions.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Manat was the greatest of these idols in rank and the most worshipped; therefore He said ﴿the third, the other﴾, emphasising her with these two attributes.

The better view is that His saying ﴿the third, the other﴾ follows the Arabic style when they report about a plurality and there is among them one who might think he is not included in the report, either because of his greatness or his remoteness from being involved in what his peers are involved in, so they conclude the report by saying: "and so-and-so is the other." Its application here is that the worshippers of Manat are numerous among the Arab tribes, so He drew attention to the fact that the multitude of its worshippers does not make it stronger than the rest of the idols in the matter of refuting its divinity, and all of this runs in the manner of mockery and disparagement.
صفحة ١٠٦
The sentence ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ is an escalation in refutation, mockery and disparagement, as has preceded, and it accords with their belief that those three idols are daughters of Allah and that the angels are daughters of Allah; meaning: do you assign to Allah daughters exclusively, while you know that you have sons, male and female, and that you prefer males and dislike females, and yet you have assigned Allah the females to the exclusion of the males, while Allah is more worthy of excellence and perfection, if you knew? In this there is additional censure of their disbelief, since it was disbelief and feebleness of intellect.

That al-Uzza and Manat were females for them is evident from the form of their names; as for al-Lat, setting aside whether the ta' in the name is taken as a feminine marker or as a root letter of the word, they used to imagine al-Lat to be female. For this reason Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said to 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi on the day of al-Hudaybiyya: "Suck the clitoris of al-Lat, or bite it."

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases in ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ is for emphasis on the exclusivity which the lam conveys, emphasis in a context of mockery and disparagement; and in fronting "wa-lahu al-unthaa" there is the indication of exclusivity, meaning: not the male.

The sentence ﴿That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ is a reason for the denial and mockery implied by the interrogation in ﴿Is the male for you...﴾, meaning: you have indeed been unjust in the division and have not been equitable, so you deserve to be denied.

The indication "that" refers to what was mentioned, by considering the report about it with the word "division," since it is feminine in form.

"Idhan" is a particle of answer, intended to answer the denial-interrogation, meaning: it follows from what you claim that it is an unjust division, that is, you have divided a division that is oppressive.

"Diza": its pattern is fu'la with a damma on the fa', from daza-hu haqqahu, meaning he diminished it, when he reduced it. The root of the 'ayn of "daza" is a hamza; it is said: da'aza-hu haqqahu, like mana'ahu, then in their speech the lightening of the hamza became common, so they said: dazahu with an alif. Its imperfect may be either ya'i or wawi in the 'ayn. Al-Kisa'i said: it is permitted to say yadiz and yadhuz. He seems to mean that you have the choice in the hamzated 'ayn when it is lightened, to make it go with waw or ya'. But the more common usage in their speech is to treat the 'ayn as ya', so they said: dazahu haqqahu dayzan, and did not say dawzan, because dawz is chewing dates in the mouth; so they wished to distinguish between the two verbal nouns, and this is one of the excellences of usage. According to al-Mu'arrij al-Sadusi, they disliked the damma on the dad in "duzaa" so they said "diza." It seems he means they found the damma on the dad heavy, that is, at the beginning of the word, though they had an alternative to it in the other pattern.

The pattern of "diza" is fu'la, an elative noun like kubra and tuba, meaning: most unjust. When the unvowelled ya' came after a damma, they vowelled it with a kasra to preserve the ya', lest they change it to waw and it become "duzaa," which is what they disliked, as al-Mu'arrij said. This is like what they did in "bid," the plural of abyad. Had they treated it as an elative from daza yadhuzu, they would have said "dawza," but they left it unused.

It has been said that the pattern of "diza" is fi'la with a kasra on the fa', as a noun, like dif'la and sh'ra, but this is weakened by the fact that it is derived, so as an adjective it is more fitting. Sibawayh said: fi'la with a kasra on the fa' does not occur as an adjective; or it is a verbal noun, like dhikra, and on both views its kasra is original.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 53, verses 19–22 (part 2 of 2):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ḍīzā (ضِيزَى) with a silent yāʾ after the ḍād, but Ibn Kathir read it with a silent hamzah after the ḍād, observing the original root of the verb, as was mentioned just before. This is a description of them as unjust, an addition to their disbelief, because thinking about injustice is like doing it, for a person's imaginings and beliefs are the heading of his thoughts and conduct.

The sentence ﴿It is nothing but names you have named﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) which returns to refute their belief from its very root, after refuting it by something that follows from it, following them in their premise in order to show the defect of their belief. In this sentence there is also a safeguard (iḥtirās) lest someone imagine that the denial concerns their attributing daughters to God, that it is a denial of their assigning daughters to God, and that He has offspring, male and female; or that the target of the denial is their claim that they are daughters, when they are not daughters, which would then be like the denial against them regarding their claim that the angels are daughters. The pronoun "hiya" (هي) refers to al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. What the pronoun refers to is the essence and reality: that is, these idols are nothing but names for which there are no named realities, and no established realities. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

The restriction (al-qasr) is relative (idafi), meaning: they are names, not rational, acting realities as you claim. The restriction is not absolute, because these idols have named referents, which are the stones or the houses to which they direct worship and for which they appoint custodians (sadana).

The sentence ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is a justification for the meaning of the restriction by way of sufficiency (al-iktifa'): that they have no realities in the world of witnessing (ʿalam al-shahadah) is a sensible matter, since they are nothing but stones. As for their having no realities from the unseen world (ʿalam al-ghayb), this is because there is no way to establish what the unseen world contains except by information from the unseen world, belonging to Him, Glorified is He, or by rational proof, such as the world's indicating the existence of the Maker and some of His attributes. God has not informed any of His messengers that the idols have spirits or angels, as He informed them about the realities of the angels, the jinn and the devils.

Sultan (سُلْطان) means proof (hujjah), and God's sending it down means informing about it. This is a metonymy (kinayah) for the absence of any proof for them, because the existence of proof necessitates its becoming manifest; so the negation of sending down proof concerning them is of the type of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not guided by, i.e., it has no landmark by which one is guided."

He expressed the revealed information by the verb "sent down" (anzala), because it is information that comes from the higher world, so it was likened to lowering a body from above to below. Likewise, he expressed the establishing of the indications of existence by "sending down", because rational reflection is among God's creation, so it was likened to sending down, as in His saying, ﴿He it is who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. Thus the use of ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is the use of a word in its two figurative meanings. In the sense of this verse is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they worship besides God what He has not sent down any authority for, and of which they have no knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj: 71] in Surah al-Hajj. And His saying in Surah Yusuf was already mentioned: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named, you and your fathers; God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

He emphasised the negation of sending down authority with the particle min (مِن) used as an extra particle, to emphasise the negation of the genus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 19–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza,﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ ﴿That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ ﴿They are but names you have named them, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

When the discussion had passed over the description of the revelation and the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) witnessing of Jibril (peace be upon him), and over what indicates the sublime matters of the greatness of Allah the Exalted and the nobility of His Messenger (ﷺ) and the nobility of Jibril (peace be upon him), in that he was described with attributes of perfection and stations of honour, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) was described with ascent through the exalted stations, this naturally evoked a comparison between these lofty states and the state of the greatest of their three gods, according to their claim, namely: al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat, which are stones whose place is the earth, having no power of disposal, and by which no one ascends to any height. Thus this opposition formed a comprehensive imaginary contrast which called for following the mention of those states with the mention of the states of these.

The discourse thus shifted from the purpose of establishing that the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed to with the Qur'an, to the refutation of idol worship. The basis of the refutation is His saying: ﴿They are but names you have named them, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The fa' (so) here is for the derivation of the interrogation and what follows it from the sentence ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12], which is derived from the sentence ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ [al-Najm: 11].

The seeing in "a-fa-ra'aytum" may be visual, transitive to one object, so it does not require a second object, and the interrogation is then one of affirmation with mockery, meaning: how do you see al-Lat

and al-Uzza and Manat in relation to what has been described of the greatness of Allah the Exalted, and the nobility of His angels and the nobility of His Messenger (ﷺ)? This is mockery of them and a refutation of the divinity of those idols by way of implication, and its evidence is direct observation. The most common usage of ara'ayta is for visual seeing, according to what Radi al-Din chose.

The sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ etc. may be a resumption and an escalation in the refutation, or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the sentence ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza﴾, since its content is among what their claims include: they used to claim that al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat were the daughters of Allah, as Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Kashshaf have related from them, and the context of the verses requires it.

It is also possible that the seeing is cognitive, meaning: do you suppose al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat [to be so]? The second object is then omitted for brevity, the indication being His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ upon it. The estimate is: you supposed them to be daughters of Allah; do you attribute to Him the female while you seek male sons? The sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ then serves as an explanation of the denial and an escalation in refuting their claims, meaning: do you assign to Allah daughters exclusively, while you take pride in male sons for yourselves?

Sahib al-Kashf made His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ take the place of the second object of "ara'aytum".

Also, since what preceded of the description of revelation and the stations of nearness in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was honoured, and the greatness of Jibril, carried an indication of the vastness of the power of Allah the Exalted and the magnitude of His dominion, which records against the polytheists, in their claim, partners to Allah—idols such as al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat—the corruption of their claim and the foolishness of their opinion, there followed the mention of indications of divine greatness with the refutation of the divinity of their idols, in that they are lower than the rank of divinity, since those are illusions that have no realities, but were invented by the imaginings of the people of polytheism, who gave them names for which there are no realities. Thus He branched off with ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza?﴾ etc. The interrogation is then one of affirmation and denial, and the seeing is cognitive, and the second object is His saying ﴿They are but names you have named them﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The sentence ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ etc. may be parenthetical between the two objects, for escalation in denial, meaning: you supposed them to be daughters of Allah, or you supposed the angels to be daughters of Allah.
صفحة ١٠٤
These aspects are not mutually exclusive, so we take them to mean that all of them are intended in this context.

You may also make the verb "ara'aytum" (on the basis that the seeing is cognitive) suspended from operating, because the negating "in" follows it in His saying ﴿They are but names you have named them﴾ [al-Najm: 23], and make the sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ up to His saying "﴿unjust﴾" a parenthetical clause.

Al-Lat: an idol that belonged to the Thaqif at al-Ta'if, which Quraysh and the majority of the Arabs worshipped, and it had fame among Quraysh. It is a square rock on which they built a structure. Al-Razi said it was in the form of a man, and it was at the place of the left minaret of the mosque of al-Ta'if; so said al-Qurtubi. Perhaps the mosque had two minarets.

The alif and lam at the beginning of al-Lat are additional, and the "al" that enters upon it is additional, and perhaps that is because its origin is "Latt," meaning "a worshipped one." When they wished to make it a proper name for a specific worshipped one, they added to it the lam of definiteness of familiarity, as in Allah, whose origin is ilah. It is pausal with the sukun on its ta' in standard Arabic.

The majority read (al-Latta) with a light taa'. Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a doubled taa', and this is a dialect for this name, since many Arabs say: the origin of its rock is a place where a man used to sit in the Jahiliyya, kneading sawiq for the pilgrims; when he died they took his place as a shrine.

Al-Uzza: the form fu'la from al-'izz (might): the name of an idol of white stone with a structure over it. Al-Razi said it was in the form of a plant; perhaps he means that the rock had in it the form of a tree. It was in the hollow of a palm tree above Dhat 'Irq. The majority of the Arabs worshipped it, especially Quraysh, and Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud, addressing the Muslims: "We have al-Uzza and you have no Uzza."

Al-Zamakhshari, in his commentary on Surat al-Fatiha, mentioned that the Arabs, when they began an action, would say: "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-Uzza."

As for Manat, it is a proper noun that is original (martajal), and it is feminine, so the rule is that it be written with the feminine ha' at its end and be paused on with the ha', and it is non-declinable. There is also a dialect with the original taa' at its end, so it is paused on with the taa' and is declinable, because the taa' of Lat is like the ba' of Bab. Its origin is manwa, with a vowel, and it may be lengthened, so one says manaa'a. It is non-declinable for being a proper name and feminine. The analogical pausal form is with the ha', but some pause with the taa' following the script of the Mushaf. It was a rock, worshipped by the majority of the Arabs, and its place was at al-Mushallal, near Qudayd between Makkah and Madinah. The Aws and the Khazraj would circumambulate around it during the Hajj instead of al-Safa and al-Marwa. When the Muslims performed Hajj and ran between al-Safa and al-Marwa, the Ansar were reluctant to run because they used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwa; then there came down concerning them His saying ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah; so whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], as has preceded from the hadith of 'A'isha in the Muwatta' in Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority read "wa-Manat" with a taa' after the alif, and Ibn Kathir read it with a hamza after the alif, according to one of the two dialects. The majority pause on it with the taa', following the orthography of the Mushaf, so the taa' is a letter of the word and not a feminine marker; it is like the taa' of al-Lat, and they make its writing in the Mushaf contrary to analogy.

Its description as "the third" is because it is third in mention, and this is a clarifying attribute; its description as "the other" is also a clarifying attribute, because its being third in mention, after the two mentioned before it, is known to the hearer. The result of the two attributes is the emphasis of its mention. This is because al-Lat and al-Uzza are more famous among Quraysh and among the majority of the Arabs than Manat, owing to the distance of Manat's place from their lands; and because the arrangement of the locations of the houses of these idols is likewise: al-Lat is in the upper Tihama at al-Ta'if, al-Uzza is in its middle at Nakhla between Makkah and al-Ta'if, and Manat is at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah, so it is the third of the regions.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Manat was the greatest of these idols in rank and the most worshipped; therefore He said ﴿the third, the other﴾, emphasising her with these two attributes.

The better view is that His saying ﴿the third, the other﴾ follows the Arabic style when they report about a plurality and there is among them one who might think he is not included in the report, either because of his greatness or his remoteness from being involved in what his peers are involved in, so they conclude the report by saying: "and so-and-so is the other." Its application here is that the worshippers of Manat are numerous among the Arab tribes, so He drew attention to the fact that the multitude of its worshippers does not make it stronger than the rest of the idols in the matter of refuting its divinity, and all of this runs in the manner of mockery and disparagement.
صفحة ١٠٦
The sentence ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ is an escalation in refutation, mockery and disparagement, as has preceded, and it accords with their belief that those three idols are daughters of Allah and that the angels are daughters of Allah; meaning: do you assign to Allah daughters exclusively, while you know that you have sons, male and female, and that you prefer males and dislike females, and yet you have assigned Allah the females to the exclusion of the males, while Allah is more worthy of excellence and perfection, if you knew? In this there is additional censure of their disbelief, since it was disbelief and feebleness of intellect.

That al-Uzza and Manat were females for them is evident from the form of their names; as for al-Lat, setting aside whether the ta' in the name is taken as a feminine marker or as a root letter of the word, they used to imagine al-Lat to be female. For this reason Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said to 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi on the day of al-Hudaybiyya: "Suck the clitoris of al-Lat, or bite it."

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases in ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ is for emphasis on the exclusivity which the lam conveys, emphasis in a context of mockery and disparagement; and in fronting "wa-lahu al-unthaa" there is the indication of exclusivity, meaning: not the male.

The sentence ﴿That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ is a reason for the denial and mockery implied by the interrogation in ﴿Is the male for you...﴾, meaning: you have indeed been unjust in the division and have not been equitable, so you deserve to be denied.

The indication "that" refers to what was mentioned, by considering the report about it with the word "division," since it is feminine in form.

"Idhan" is a particle of answer, intended to answer the denial-interrogation, meaning: it follows from what you claim that it is an unjust division, that is, you have divided a division that is oppressive.

"Diza": its pattern is fu'la with a damma on the fa', from daza-hu haqqahu, meaning he diminished it, when he reduced it. The root of the 'ayn of "daza" is a hamza; it is said: da'aza-hu haqqahu, like mana'ahu, then in their speech the lightening of the hamza became common, so they said: dazahu with an alif. Its imperfect may be either ya'i or wawi in the 'ayn. Al-Kisa'i said: it is permitted to say yadiz and yadhuz. He seems to mean that you have the choice in the hamzated 'ayn when it is lightened, to make it go with waw or ya'. But the more common usage in their speech is to treat the 'ayn as ya', so they said: dazahu haqqahu dayzan, and did not say dawzan, because dawz is chewing dates in the mouth; so they wished to distinguish between the two verbal nouns, and this is one of the excellences of usage. According to al-Mu'arrij al-Sadusi, they disliked the damma on the dad in "duzaa" so they said "diza." It seems he means they found the damma on the dad heavy, that is, at the beginning of the word, though they had an alternative to it in the other pattern.

The pattern of "diza" is fu'la, an elative noun like kubra and tuba, meaning: most unjust. When the unvowelled ya' came after a damma, they vowelled it with a kasra to preserve the ya', lest they change it to waw and it become "duzaa," which is what they disliked, as al-Mu'arrij said. This is like what they did in "bid," the plural of abyad. Had they treated it as an elative from daza yadhuzu, they would have said "dawza," but they left it unused.

It has been said that the pattern of "diza" is fi'la with a kasra on the fa', as a noun, like dif'la and sh'ra, but this is weakened by the fact that it is derived, so as an adjective it is more fitting. Sibawayh said: fi'la with a kasra on the fa' does not occur as an adjective; or it is a verbal noun, like dhikra, and on both views its kasra is original.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 53, verses 19–22 (part 2 of 2):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ḍīzā (ضِيزَى) with a silent yāʾ after the ḍād, but Ibn Kathir read it with a silent hamzah after the ḍād, observing the original root of the verb, as was mentioned just before. This is a description of them as unjust, an addition to their disbelief, because thinking about injustice is like doing it, for a person's imaginings and beliefs are the heading of his thoughts and conduct.

The sentence ﴿It is nothing but names you have named﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) which returns to refute their belief from its very root, after refuting it by something that follows from it, following them in their premise in order to show the defect of their belief. In this sentence there is also a safeguard (iḥtirās) lest someone imagine that the denial concerns their attributing daughters to God, that it is a denial of their assigning daughters to God, and that He has offspring, male and female; or that the target of the denial is their claim that they are daughters, when they are not daughters, which would then be like the denial against them regarding their claim that the angels are daughters. The pronoun "hiya" (هي) refers to al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. What the pronoun refers to is the essence and reality: that is, these idols are nothing but names for which there are no named realities, and no established realities. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

The restriction (al-qasr) is relative (idafi), meaning: they are names, not rational, acting realities as you claim. The restriction is not absolute, because these idols have named referents, which are the stones or the houses to which they direct worship and for which they appoint custodians (sadana).

The sentence ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is a justification for the meaning of the restriction by way of sufficiency (al-iktifa'): that they have no realities in the world of witnessing (ʿalam al-shahadah) is a sensible matter, since they are nothing but stones. As for their having no realities from the unseen world (ʿalam al-ghayb), this is because there is no way to establish what the unseen world contains except by information from the unseen world, belonging to Him, Glorified is He, or by rational proof, such as the world's indicating the existence of the Maker and some of His attributes. God has not informed any of His messengers that the idols have spirits or angels, as He informed them about the realities of the angels, the jinn and the devils.

Sultan (سُلْطان) means proof (hujjah), and God's sending it down means informing about it. This is a metonymy (kinayah) for the absence of any proof for them, because the existence of proof necessitates its becoming manifest; so the negation of sending down proof concerning them is of the type of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not guided by, i.e., it has no landmark by which one is guided."

He expressed the revealed information by the verb "sent down" (anzala), because it is information that comes from the higher world, so it was likened to lowering a body from above to below. Likewise, he expressed the establishing of the indications of existence by "sending down", because rational reflection is among God's creation, so it was likened to sending down, as in His saying, ﴿He it is who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. Thus the use of ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is the use of a word in its two figurative meanings. In the sense of this verse is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they worship besides God what He has not sent down any authority for, and of which they have no knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj: 71] in Surah al-Hajj. And His saying in Surah Yusuf was already mentioned: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named, you and your fathers; God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

He emphasised the negation of sending down authority with the particle min (مِن) used as an extra particle, to emphasise the negation of the genus.
