Its description as "the third" is because it is third in mention, and this is a clarifying attribute; its description as "the other" is also a clarifying attribute, because its being third in mention, after the two mentioned before it, is known to the hearer. The result of the two attributes is the emphasis of its mention. This is because al-Lat and al-Uzza are more famous among Quraysh and among the majority of the Arabs than Manat, owing to the distance of Manat's place from their lands; and because the arrangement of the locations of the houses of these idols is likewise: al-Lat is in the upper Tihama at al-Ta'if, al-Uzza is in its middle at Nakhla between Makkah and al-Ta'if, and Manat is at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah, so it is the third of the regions.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Manat was the greatest of these idols in rank and the most worshipped; therefore He said ﴿the third, the other﴾, emphasising her with these two attributes.

The better view is that His saying ﴿the third, the other﴾ follows the Arabic style when they report about a plurality and there is among them one who might think he is not included in the report, either because of his greatness or his remoteness from being involved in what his peers are involved in, so they conclude the report by saying: "and so-and-so is the other." Its application here is that the worshippers of Manat are numerous among the Arab tribes, so He drew attention to the fact that the multitude of its worshippers does not make it stronger than the rest of the idols in the matter of refuting its divinity, and all of this runs in the manner of mockery and disparagement.
صفحة ١٠٦
The sentence ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ is an escalation in refutation, mockery and disparagement, as has preceded, and it accords with their belief that those three idols are daughters of Allah and that the angels are daughters of Allah; meaning: do you assign to Allah daughters exclusively, while you know that you have sons, male and female, and that you prefer males and dislike females, and yet you have assigned Allah the females to the exclusion of the males, while Allah is more worthy of excellence and perfection, if you knew? In this there is additional censure of their disbelief, since it was disbelief and feebleness of intellect.

That al-Uzza and Manat were females for them is evident from the form of their names; as for al-Lat, setting aside whether the ta' in the name is taken as a feminine marker or as a root letter of the word, they used to imagine al-Lat to be female. For this reason Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said to 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi on the day of al-Hudaybiyya: "Suck the clitoris of al-Lat, or bite it."

The fronting of the two prepositional phrases in ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ is for emphasis on the exclusivity which the lam conveys, emphasis in a context of mockery and disparagement; and in fronting "wa-lahu al-unthaa" there is the indication of exclusivity, meaning: not the male.

The sentence ﴿That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ is a reason for the denial and mockery implied by the interrogation in ﴿Is the male for you...﴾, meaning: you have indeed been unjust in the division and have not been equitable, so you deserve to be denied.

The indication "that" refers to what was mentioned, by considering the report about it with the word "division," since it is feminine in form.

"Idhan" is a particle of answer, intended to answer the denial-interrogation, meaning: it follows from what you claim that it is an unjust division, that is, you have divided a division that is oppressive.

"Diza": its pattern is fu'la with a damma on the fa', from daza-hu haqqahu, meaning he diminished it, when he reduced it. The root of the 'ayn of "daza" is a hamza; it is said: da'aza-hu haqqahu, like mana'ahu, then in their speech the lightening of the hamza became common, so they said: dazahu with an alif. Its imperfect may be either ya'i or wawi in the 'ayn. Al-Kisa'i said: it is permitted to say yadiz and yadhuz. He seems to mean that you have the choice in the hamzated 'ayn when it is lightened, to make it go with waw or ya'. But the more common usage in their speech is to treat the 'ayn as ya', so they said: dazahu haqqahu dayzan, and did not say dawzan, because dawz is chewing dates in the mouth; so they wished to distinguish between the two verbal nouns, and this is one of the excellences of usage. According to al-Mu'arrij al-Sadusi, they disliked the damma on the dad in "duzaa" so they said "diza." It seems he means they found the damma on the dad heavy, that is, at the beginning of the word, though they had an alternative to it in the other pattern.

The pattern of "diza" is fu'la, an elative noun like kubra and tuba, meaning: most unjust. When the unvowelled ya' came after a damma, they vowelled it with a kasra to preserve the ya', lest they change it to waw and it become "duzaa," which is what they disliked, as al-Mu'arrij said. This is like what they did in "bid," the plural of abyad. Had they treated it as an elative from daza yadhuzu, they would have said "dawza," but they left it unused.

It has been said that the pattern of "diza" is fi'la with a kasra on the fa', as a noun, like dif'la and sh'ra, but this is weakened by the fact that it is derived, so as an adjective it is more fitting. Sibawayh said: fi'la with a kasra on the fa' does not occur as an adjective; or it is a verbal noun, like dhikra, and on both views its kasra is original.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 53, verses 19–22 (part 2 of 2):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ḍīzā (ضِيزَى) with a silent yāʾ after the ḍād, but Ibn Kathir read it with a silent hamzah after the ḍād, observing the original root of the verb, as was mentioned just before. This is a description of them as unjust, an addition to their disbelief, because thinking about injustice is like doing it, for a person's imaginings and beliefs are the heading of his thoughts and conduct.

The sentence ﴿It is nothing but names you have named﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) which returns to refute their belief from its very root, after refuting it by something that follows from it, following them in their premise in order to show the defect of their belief. In this sentence there is also a safeguard (iḥtirās) lest someone imagine that the denial concerns their attributing daughters to God, that it is a denial of their assigning daughters to God, and that He has offspring, male and female; or that the target of the denial is their claim that they are daughters, when they are not daughters, which would then be like the denial against them regarding their claim that the angels are daughters. The pronoun "hiya" (هي) refers to al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. What the pronoun refers to is the essence and reality: that is, these idols are nothing but names for which there are no named realities, and no established realities. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

The restriction (al-qasr) is relative (idafi), meaning: they are names, not rational, acting realities as you claim. The restriction is not absolute, because these idols have named referents, which are the stones or the houses to which they direct worship and for which they appoint custodians (sadana).

The sentence ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is a justification for the meaning of the restriction by way of sufficiency (al-iktifa'): that they have no realities in the world of witnessing (ʿalam al-shahadah) is a sensible matter, since they are nothing but stones. As for their having no realities from the unseen world (ʿalam al-ghayb), this is because there is no way to establish what the unseen world contains except by information from the unseen world, belonging to Him, Glorified is He, or by rational proof, such as the world's indicating the existence of the Maker and some of His attributes. God has not informed any of His messengers that the idols have spirits or angels, as He informed them about the realities of the angels, the jinn and the devils.

Sultan (سُلْطان) means proof (hujjah), and God's sending it down means informing about it. This is a metonymy (kinayah) for the absence of any proof for them, because the existence of proof necessitates its becoming manifest; so the negation of sending down proof concerning them is of the type of the line of poetry: "On a road whose landmarks are not guided by, i.e., it has no landmark by which one is guided."

He expressed the revealed information by the verb "sent down" (anzala), because it is information that comes from the higher world, so it was likened to lowering a body from above to below. Likewise, he expressed the establishing of the indications of existence by "sending down", because rational reflection is among God's creation, so it was likened to sending down, as in His saying, ﴿He it is who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. Thus the use of ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [al-Najm: 23] is the use of a word in its two figurative meanings. In the sense of this verse is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they worship besides God what He has not sent down any authority for, and of which they have no knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj: 71] in Surah al-Hajj. And His saying in Surah Yusuf was already mentioned: ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named, you and your fathers; God has sent down no authority for them﴾ [Yusuf: 40].

He emphasised the negation of sending down authority with the particle min (مِن) used as an extra particle, to emphasise the negation of the genus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 19–22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza,﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ ﴿That, then, is an unjust division!﴾ ﴿They are but names you have named them, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

When the discussion had passed over the description of the revelation and the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) witnessing of Jibril (peace be upon him), and over what indicates the sublime matters of the greatness of Allah the Exalted and the nobility of His Messenger (ﷺ) and the nobility of Jibril (peace be upon him), in that he was described with attributes of perfection and stations of honour, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) was described with ascent through the exalted stations, this naturally evoked a comparison between these lofty states and the state of the greatest of their three gods, according to their claim, namely: al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat, which are stones whose place is the earth, having no power of disposal, and by which no one ascends to any height. Thus this opposition formed a comprehensive imaginary contrast which called for following the mention of those states with the mention of the states of these.

The discourse thus shifted from the purpose of establishing that the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed to with the Qur'an, to the refutation of idol worship. The basis of the refutation is His saying: ﴿They are but names you have named them, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The fa' (so) here is for the derivation of the interrogation and what follows it from the sentence ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12], which is derived from the sentence ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ [al-Najm: 11].

The seeing in "a-fa-ra'aytum" may be visual, transitive to one object, so it does not require a second object, and the interrogation is then one of affirmation with mockery, meaning: how do you see al-Lat
صفحة ١٠٣
and al-Uzza and Manat in relation to what has been described of the greatness of Allah the Exalted, and the nobility of His angels and the nobility of His Messenger (ﷺ)? This is mockery of them and a refutation of the divinity of those idols by way of implication, and its evidence is direct observation. The most common usage of ara'ayta is for visual seeing, according to what Radi al-Din chose.

The sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ etc. may be a resumption and an escalation in the refutation, or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the sentence ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza﴾, since its content is among what their claims include: they used to claim that al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat were the daughters of Allah, as Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Kashshaf have related from them, and the context of the verses requires it.

It is also possible that the seeing is cognitive, meaning: do you suppose al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat [to be so]? The second object is then omitted for brevity, the indication being His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ upon it. The estimate is: you supposed them to be daughters of Allah; do you attribute to Him the female while you seek male sons? The sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ then serves as an explanation of the denial and an escalation in refuting their claims, meaning: do you assign to Allah daughters exclusively, while you take pride in male sons for yourselves?

Sahib al-Kashf made His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ take the place of the second object of "ara'aytum".

Also, since what preceded of the description of revelation and the stations of nearness in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was honoured, and the greatness of Jibril, carried an indication of the vastness of the power of Allah the Exalted and the magnitude of His dominion, which records against the polytheists, in their claim, partners to Allah—idols such as al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat—the corruption of their claim and the foolishness of their opinion, there followed the mention of indications of divine greatness with the refutation of the divinity of their idols, in that they are lower than the rank of divinity, since those are illusions that have no realities, but were invented by the imaginings of the people of polytheism, who gave them names for which there are no realities. Thus He branched off with ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza?﴾ etc. The interrogation is then one of affirmation and denial, and the seeing is cognitive, and the second object is His saying ﴿They are but names you have named them﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The sentence ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ etc. may be parenthetical between the two objects, for escalation in denial, meaning: you supposed them to be daughters of Allah, or you supposed the angels to be daughters of Allah.
صفحة ١٠٤
These aspects are not mutually exclusive, so we take them to mean that all of them are intended in this context.

You may also make the verb "ara'aytum" (on the basis that the seeing is cognitive) suspended from operating, because the negating "in" follows it in His saying ﴿They are but names you have named them﴾ [al-Najm: 23], and make the sentence ﴿Is the male for you...﴾ up to His saying "﴿unjust﴾" a parenthetical clause.

Al-Lat: an idol that belonged to the Thaqif at al-Ta'if, which Quraysh and the majority of the Arabs worshipped, and it had fame among Quraysh. It is a square rock on which they built a structure. Al-Razi said it was in the form of a man, and it was at the place of the left minaret of the mosque of al-Ta'if; so said al-Qurtubi. Perhaps the mosque had two minarets.

The alif and lam at the beginning of al-Lat are additional, and the "al" that enters upon it is additional, and perhaps that is because its origin is "Latt," meaning "a worshipped one." When they wished to make it a proper name for a specific worshipped one, they added to it the lam of definiteness of familiarity, as in Allah, whose origin is ilah. It is pausal with the sukun on its ta' in standard Arabic.

The majority read (al-Latta) with a light taa'. Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a doubled taa', and this is a dialect for this name, since many Arabs say: the origin of its rock is a place where a man used to sit in the Jahiliyya, kneading sawiq for the pilgrims; when he died they took his place as a shrine.

Al-Uzza: the form fu'la from al-'izz (might): the name of an idol of white stone with a structure over it. Al-Razi said it was in the form of a plant; perhaps he means that the rock had in it the form of a tree. It was in the hollow of a palm tree above Dhat 'Irq. The majority of the Arabs worshipped it, especially Quraysh, and Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud, addressing the Muslims: "We have al-Uzza and you have no Uzza."

Al-Zamakhshari, in his commentary on Surat al-Fatiha, mentioned that the Arabs, when they began an action, would say: "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-Uzza."

As for Manat, it is a proper noun that is original (martajal), and it is feminine, so the rule is that it be written with the feminine ha' at its end and be paused on with the ha', and it is non-declinable. There is also a dialect with the original taa' at its end, so it is paused on with the taa' and is declinable, because the taa' of Lat is like the ba' of Bab. Its origin is manwa, with a vowel, and it may be lengthened, so one says manaa'a. It is non-declinable for being a proper name and feminine. The analogical pausal form is with the ha', but some pause with the taa' following the script of the Mushaf. It was a rock, worshipped by the majority of the Arabs, and its place was at al-Mushallal, near Qudayd between Makkah and Madinah. The Aws and the Khazraj would circumambulate around it during the Hajj instead of al-Safa and al-Marwa. When the Muslims performed Hajj and ran between al-Safa and al-Marwa, the Ansar were reluctant to run because they used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwa; then there came down concerning them His saying ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah; so whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], as has preceded from the hadith of 'A'isha in the Muwatta' in Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority pause on it with the taa', following the orthography of the Mushaf, so the taa' is a letter of the word and not a feminine marker; it is like the taa' of al-Lat, and they make its writing in the Mushaf contrary to analogy.

Its description as "the third" is because it is third in mention, and this is a clarifying attribute; its description as "the other" is also a clarifying attribute, because its being third in mention, after the two mentioned before it, is known to the hearer. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 23:

[109]
﴿They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord.﴾
This is a shift away from addressing the polytheists, which had begun from the start of the surah, and it is one of the forms of iltifat (shift of address). It is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), so the pronoun in "yattabi'una" (they follow) refers back to those to whom the address had been directed.

It follows the negation that they have any proof for the attributes they claim for their idols, or for the claim that God named them with those names, by affirming that in what they claim they rely on illusions and on what their souls love: the worship of idols, the devotion of their custodians, the processions of visiting them, and their delusion that these idols intercede for them with God Most High in ways that suit their desires in this life. These are illusions and cherished wishes, and they live in the deception of them.

The imperfect "yattabi'una" is used to indicate that they will continue to follow conjecture and what their souls desire, and this indicates that they had followed that before, by the implication of the wording (lahn al-khitab) or its meaning (fahwa).

The basic meaning of zann (conjecture) is belief that is not certain, and it is also applied to certain knowledge when it concerns unseen matters, as in His saying ﴿those who think (yazunnuna) that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is frequently used in the Qur'an for false belief, as in His saying ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116] in Surat al-An'am. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of conjecture, for conjecture is the most false of speech." This is the meaning intended here, by the evidence of the conjunction of "and what their souls desire" to it, just as "and they are only guessing" [al-An'am: 116] was conjoined to its counterpart in Surat al-An'am. It is a metonymy for error, in view of its frequent connection to it, as He, the Exalted, said ﴿O you who believe, avoid much conjecture, for indeed some conjecture is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12].

This variety in the meanings of zann in the Qur'an points to the obligation to examine the matter that is conjectured, until the Muslim attaches it to what suits it of praise or blame according to the evidences. Therefore our scholars deduced that conjecture does not suffice in establishing the fundamentals of belief, and that correct conjecture is the basis on which the branches of the Sharia rest.

[110]
What is meant by "what their souls desire" is that for which there is no motive except inclination of desire, apart from evidences. If the beloved thing has been shown by evidences to be true, its love only increases it in acceptance, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Two men who love each other for the sake of God, meet upon it and part upon it; and a man whose heart is attached to the mosques." And he said: "The coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer."
Thus the basis of blame in this verse is restricting their following to what their souls desire.

Furthermore, zann in dealings between people and in moral dispositions of the soul has rulings and degrees other than its status in religious matters, its roots and its branches. Some of it is praiseworthy and some blameworthy, as He, the Exalted, said ﴿Indeed, some conjecture is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. It has been said: grief is bad conjecture about people.

The definiteness in "al-anfus" is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning "what their souls desire," and "ma" is a relative pronoun.

The conjunction of "and what their souls desire" to "conjecture" is a conjunction of cause to effect, meaning: the conjecture that moves them to follow it is that it agrees with their guidance and their habits.

The clause "and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord" is a circumstantial clause (hal) confirming the wonder at their condition, meaning: they continue to follow conjecture and desire while God has sent to them a messenger with guidance.

The oath particle (lam al-qasam) is for emphasis of the report, for the sake of intensifying the wonder at their condition contained in it, as if the addressee doubted whether there had come to them what contains a guidance convincing to them, given their persistence in their error in a way that such persistence is not thought to be possible in a sensible person.

The expression of the Majesty by the title "their Lord" is to increase the wonder at their deafness to hearing guidance, although He is one whose obedience is obligatory. Thus their error was mixed with disobedience and rebellion against their Creator.

The definiteness in "al-huda" is to indicate the meaning of perfection, that is, the clear guidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 24–25:

Page 111
﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ ﴿But to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾

This is a transitional digression (idrab intiqali) arising from His saying: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

The interrogation implied after "am" (or) is a denial (istifham inkari), intended to nullify man's attainment of whatever he wishes for, and to nullify his making what he wishes for the motive behind his deeds and beliefs. Rather, he must seek the truth through its proofs and signs, even if it opposes what he wishes. This is connected to His saying: ﴿They follow only assumption and what the souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23].

This is a discipline and training of the souls to bear what opposes their desires when the truth contradicts their whims, and he should compel himself to it until it becomes part of his character.

The definiteness of "al-insan" (man) is generic (ta'rif al-jins), and its occurrence within the scope of the denial, which is equivalent to negation, makes it general to every human being.

The relative pronoun in ﴿what he wished﴾ is in the position of a noun defined by the generic al-, and its occurrence within the scope of the denial interrogation, which is equivalent to negation, requires generality. That is: man has nothing of what he wishes; that is, the matter does not proceed according to his will but according to the will of Allah. This includes every desire that called them to turn away from the words of the Messenger (ﷺ), and so it includes their wish for the intercession of the idols, which is the most important of their concerns regarding the idols. This is confirmed by His saying after this: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession does not avail at all﴾ [al-Najm: 26], and their wish that the Messenger be an angel, and other things like their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], and their saying: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yunus: 15].

It follows from the denial that Allah is the Owner of the Hereafter and the first life; that is, He disposes of the states of their people according to His will, not according to man's wishes. This nullifies the beliefs of the polytheists, among which is their certainty in the intercession of their idols.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿for man what he wishes﴾ is because the focus of the denial is their wish that matters proceed according to their desires; therefore they turned away from everything that opposed their desires. Fronting the complement here serves to restrict (qasr), and it is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb): that is, this is not restricted to them as their situation requires, so they are treated as those who see matters proceeding according to what they wish. That is: rather, human wishes are in the hand of Allah, He gives some of them and withholds others, as indicated by the consequent branching in His saying: ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾

This is one of the meanings of wisdom, because man's desire that what he wishes for be attained is a desire which, if its holder reflected upon it, he would find its realization impossible, since what one person wishes for, others also wish for, so wishes conflict. If what one wishes for is given to one person, whoever else wishes for the same is deprived, and this leads to frustrating both wishes in the Hereafter. The law by which Allah established the order of this existence is that shares are apportioned, and each person has a portion; it is incumbent upon the wise person to cultivate contentment with this, otherwise people would live in bitter hardship. In the hadith: "A woman should not ask for the divorce of her sister in order to empty her bowl, and so that she may [take her place]; for she will have only what has been written for her."

The branching ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾ is an explicit statement of the concept of the restricted restriction (qasr idafi), as you have learned just above. The fronting of the prepositional phrase serves to restrict: to Allah, not to man.

"Al-Akhirah" is the otherworldly realm, and "al-Ula" is the worldly realm. What is meant by them is what they contain of matters, that is: the matters of the Hereafter and the matters of the first life. The purpose of mentioning them is to generalize all things, like His saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17].

The Hereafter was placed first for emphasis on it, and the dual form notwithstanding, it is the one to which the concern of the believers must be directed; because the address in this verse is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, along with what this placement contains of consideration for the rhyme (fasila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 26:

﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah permits it for whom He wills and approves.﴾

When Allah had made clear that the affairs of both abodes are in the hand of Allah, the Exalted, and that man does not have what he wishes, He gave as an example one of the wishes most cherished by the polytheists, namely their saying about the idols: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and their saying ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18].

Page 113

He then refuted their saying by way of the implication of the discourse (fahwa al-khitab), namely that the angels, who have the honour of rank, since the angels are among the inhabitants of the heavens, cannot deny that they are more noble than the idols. They do not possess intercession except when Allah permits that one be interceded for, whenever He wills to accept the intercession on behalf of the one for whom it is made. How then could the polytheists have what they wished of the intercession of the idols for them, those who say ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18], when they are stones on the earth and not angels in the heavens? Thus it is established that there is no intercession except for whom Allah wills, and Allah has negated the intercession of the idols, so the belief of the polytheists that they are their intercessors is nullified. This is the reason for the coordination (ʿatf) of this sentence upon the sentence ﴿Or does man have what he wishes?﴾ [al-Najm: 24]. This transition is not an abrupt one (iqtida'), but is made to explain the greatness of the matter of intercession.

"Kam" (how many) is a noun indicating a large number, and it is the subject (mubtada'), while the predicate (khabar) is ﴿whose intercession will avail nothing﴾.

The discussion of "kam" has already been mentioned in Allah's saying ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4] in al-A'raf.

"Fi al-samawat" (in the heavens) is a qualifier (sifah) of "malak" (angel). Its purpose is to express the nobility of the angels through the nobility of the world of which they are the inhabitants, namely the world of virtues and the abodes of mysteries.

The clause ﴿whose intercession will avail nothing﴾ etc. is the predicate of "kam," meaning: the intercession of any one of them will avail nothing. It is general because the verb occurs in a context of negation, and because the intercession is attributed to their pronoun, meaning: all the angels, despite their multitude and elevated rank, the intercession of not one of them will avail.

"Shay'an" (anything) is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) for generalisation, meaning: anything at all of availing, to add emphasis on the generality of the negation of the availing of their intercession.

Since the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿whose intercession will avail nothing﴾ may give the impression that they might intercede and their intercession is then not accepted, and that is not intended, because what is meant is that they do not dare to intercede before Allah, therefore He follows it with the exception in His saying ﴿except after Allah permits for whom He wills and approves﴾. This is what His saying ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28], and His saying ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], require, meaning: except after Allah grants permission to one of them to intercede and approves of the acceptance of it on behalf of the one for whom intercession is made.

Therefore, the intended meaning of "man yashi'" (whom He wills) is those whom Allah wills from among them, meaning: when He grants permission to one of them, his intercession is accepted. The lam in His saying ﴿li-man yasha'﴾ is the lam that follows the root of intercession (shafa'ah) before the one interceded for, so it is connected with their intercession, in the manner of His saying ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]; the lam is not connected with ﴿Allah permits﴾. The object of "ya'dhanu" (permits) is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿whose intercession will avail nothing﴾. Its estimated form is: that Allah permits them.

It is also permissible that the lam be for transitivity of "ya'dhanu," since it is intended with the meaning of "yastami'" (listens), meaning: that He makes known to whom He wills of them that He accepts from him. The meaning of this is that the angels continually draw near by seeking to elevate the believers to the highest ranks, as indicated by His saying ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], and His saying ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. For seeking forgiveness is supplication, while intercession is a higher kind of direction. So when Allah wills to answer their supplication for some of the believers, the angels know that one of them is permitted to intercede for him before Allah, and he intercedes, and his intercession is accepted. This is an approximation of the manner of intercession. A parallel to this is what is related in the hadith of the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Day of Gathering.

"Wa-yarda" (and approves) is coordinated (ʿutifa) upon ﴿li-man yasha'﴾ to indicate that Allah's permission for intercession follows His will, when the one interceded for is worthy of being interceded for. In this ambiguity there is an exhortation to the believers to strive to seek the pleasure of Allah, so that they may be worthy of pardon for what they have neglected of deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾ ﴿And they have no knowledge of it.﴾ [al-Najm: 27–28].

This is a digression (i'tiradh wa istitrad) occasioned by the mention of the angels, and it follows from what was mentioned just before, namely the polytheists' making al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat daughters of God, through His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [al-Najm: 19] up to His saying ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ [al-Najm: 21]. The reins of refutation and nullification are turned back toward them, combining the refutation of two similar falsehoods: their claim that the angels are daughters of God. The apparent expectation was that those being refuted be referred to by a pronoun of the third person, following His saying ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾ [al-Najm: 28]. Instead, there is a shift from the pronoun to an explicit noun phrase through the relative pronoun (al-mawsuliyyah), because of what the relative clause (al-silah) indicates of rebuke for them and belittling of their beliefs, since they disbelieved in the Hereafter, a matter that had been conveyed repeatedly on the tongues of the messengers and among the adherents of the religions neighboring them: the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. So the relative form here is used for belittling and mockery, like God's report about them: ﴿And they said: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad!﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]. However, the mockery reported there is the mockery of the falsifier toward the one who is right, because they do not believe that the relative clause's content occurs. As for the mockery here, it is the mockery of the one who is right toward the falsifier, because the content of the relative clause is established for them.

The word "naming" (tasmiyah) here is used absolutely in the sense of description (tawsif), because the noun (ism) may be applied to the word that signifies a meaning, and it may be applied to the signified named thing, whether a being or a meaning, as in the verse of Labid:

"Until the year is complete, and the greeting of peace upon you both,"

i.e., "the peace upon you both." And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1]; and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a spring therein called Salsabil﴾ [al-Insan: 18], i.e., it is described by this attribute in the goodness of its return; and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do you know anyone with His name?﴾ [Maryam: 65], i.e., there is no equal to God. Its explanation has already passed in full detail at the commentary on ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Fatihah: 1] at the beginning of al-Fatihah.

The meaning is: they claim the angels to be females, and that is a description. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. They used to say: the angels are daughters of God, from the noblest of the jinn. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they said: The Most Merciful has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26], and He said: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158].

The definiteness in "al-unthā" (the female) is the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), which carries the sense of plurality. What prompted this arrangement is the observance of the rhyme-endings (fawasil), so that the word unthā falls as a rhyme-ending, just as the word ula (the first) fell, and the word yarda (He is pleased) and the word shay'an (anything).

The clause ﴿And they have no knowledge of it﴾ [al-Najm: 28] is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in yusammunna (they name): that is, they attribute to the angels the attributes of females while they have no knowledge of that; it is merely imagination and delusion, since knowledge is only attained through evidence, and they have no evidence. Thus the negation of knowledge is intended to mean the negation of it, and the negation of evidence, by way of metonymy (al-kinayah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 28:

Page 116
﴿They follow nothing but conjecture, and indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth.﴾

The position of this sentence has several aspects. It contains an explanation of the sentence "and they have no knowledge of it" and a return to the sentence "They follow nothing but conjecture and what the souls desire," as well as a confirmation of its content and a preparation for the consequence "So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance."

The word "following" (al-ittiba') is used figuratively for adopting a thing and holding to what it requires, meaning: they take in this matter only the evidence of mistaken conjecture.

The word "conjecture" (al-zann) is applied to mistaken belief, as is its most common usage, with the indication of His words after it, ﴿and indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. A parallel of this was mentioned just before.

The term "conjecture" is stated explicitly rather than by a pronoun so that the sentence stands on its own and proceeds like a proverb.

Negating "avail" (al-ighna') means negating benefit, i.e., it benefits nothing of the truth. So the particle "min" (from) is explicative (bayan), and it precedes what it specifies, namely "shay'an" (anything).

"Shay'an" is in the accusative as the object of "yughni" (avails).

The meaning: the truth is the realities of things as they are, and apprehending them is knowledge (defined as the conception of the known as it actually is). Conjecture by itself does not yield that apprehension; so if it happens to coincide with the truth, that is by chance and coincidence, especially mistaken conjecture as here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 29:

﴿So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance and desire nothing but the worldly life.﴾ ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge.﴾ [al-Najm: 30].

After describing their false perceptions and their misguidance, He made a consequence of it the command to His Prophet ﷺ to turn away from them. This is because what preceded of the description of their misguidance was the result of their turning away from the remembrance of Allah, which is the turning away from the reminder. It is therefore fitting that their recompense for that turning away be a turning away from them. The turning away (i'rad) and the turning away (tawalli) are synonymous or near-synonymous. So what is meant by "those who turn away" (man tawalla) is the group who turned away from the Qur'an, namely those addressed just before in His words ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2] and His words ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ [al-Najm: 19], and those spoken of in His words ﴿They follow nothing but assumption﴾ [al-Najm: 23], etc., and His words ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Najm: 27], etc.

Both i'rad and tawalli are used here in their figurative sense. As for i'rad, it is borrowed for abandoning argument or for ceasing to care about their safety from punishment and the anger of Allah. As for tawalli, it is borrowed for not listening or for not complying.

The literal meaning of i'rad is turning the face away from something, since it is derived from al-'arid, which is the side of the cheek, because one who dislikes something turns his face away from it.

The literal meaning of tawalli is retreating and departing. The turning away of the Prophet ﷺ from them, which he was commanded to do, is intended to mean not caring about their salvation, because they did not accept guidance. Otherwise, the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to continue calling them to faith. Just as he used to call them before the revelation of this verse, he called them many times after its revelation. Moreover, the call is not restricted to them, for the believers benefit from it, and those among the polytheists from whom no turning away has yet proceeded will hear what the ones who turn away are warned of, and will reflect upon what the verses of the Qur'an describe them as. By this you know that this verse and its like have no connection with abandonment, nor is it abrogated by the verses of fighting.

The discussion of this has already preceded in His words ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surah al-Nisa', and in His words ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 106] in Surah al-An'am, so add to it what is here.

As for what the phrase "man tawalla" refers to, it is the people who turned away. The verb came in the singular form out of regard for the word "man" (who). Do you not see His saying "That is the extent of their knowledge," using the plural pronoun?

The explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun, so it says "So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance" rather than "So turn away from them," because the relative clause indicates the reason for the command to turn away from them, and that their turning away from the remembrance of Allah is a consequence of the misguidance whose description preceded, since their being described with turning away from the remembrance had not been mentioned before; rather, only the causes of it had been described.

The remembrance (dhikr) attributed to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is the Qur'an.

The meaning of "and desire nothing but the worldly life" is a metonym for not believing in the Hereafter, as indicated by His words "That is the extent of their knowledge" [al-Najm: 30], for if they believed in it in its reality, they would desire it, even through some of their deeds.

The clause "That is the extent of their knowledge" is an interjection (i'tiraD), and it is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) by which the cause of their ignorance of the existence of the Hereafter is clarified, because it is strange to what the questioner would ask about; and in it is contempt and disdain for them by the smallness of their knowledge.

This resumption occurred as an interjection between the sentences and their cause in His words "Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way" [al-Najm: 30], and so on.

I mean the essence of His words "and desire nothing but the worldly life."

His words "That" (dhalika) are a reference to what was mentioned in the preceding statement, His words "and desire nothing but the worldly life." The name of the boundary that the traveler reaches is borrowed for the thing they did not know, so that they know nothing of what lies beyond it of lands.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 30–31:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided.﴾

This is a justification (ta'lil) for the clause "So turn away from those who turn away," and it is a consolation (tasliyah) for the Prophet (ﷺ). The statement is used, by way of metonymy (kinayah), to mean that He is the one who takes charge of their reckoning and their recompense, and within it is a warning (wa'id) to those who go astray. The emphasis conveyed by "inna" (indeed) and by the pronoun of separation refers to the metaphorical meaning. As for His being most knowing of this, there is no requirement for emphasis with "inna," since the one addressed is the Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning is: He knows their condition better than you do.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) conveys restriction (qasr), and it is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi). The meaning is: you do not know their inner states, so do not grieve over them.

Page 119

The clause "and He is most knowing of who is guided" is a completion (tatmim), and in it is a promise (wa'd) to the believers and good tidings (bishara) to the Prophet (ﷺ). The letter "ba'" (bi) in "bi-man dalla" and in "bi-manih-tada" serves to make the two attributes of "a'lam" (most knowing) transitive, and it denotes association (mulabasah). That is, He is more knowing, associated with those who have strayed from His way, meaning associated with the state of this situation. As for the mention of those who are guided, it is a completion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 30–31:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided.﴾

This is a justification (ta'lil) for the clause "So turn away from those who turn away," and it is a consolation (tasliyah) for the Prophet (ﷺ). The statement is used, by way of metonymy (kinayah), to mean that He is the one who takes charge of their reckoning and their recompense, and within it is a warning (wa'id) to those who go astray. The emphasis conveyed by "inna" (indeed) and by the pronoun of separation refers to the metaphorical meaning. As for His being most knowing of this, there is no requirement for emphasis with "inna," since the one addressed is the Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning is: He knows their condition better than you do.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) conveys restriction (qasr), and it is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi). The meaning is: you do not know their inner states, so do not grieve over them.

Page 119

The clause "and He is most knowing of who is guided" is a completion (tatmim), and in it is a promise (wa'd) to the believers and good tidings (bishara) to the Prophet (ﷺ). The letter "ba'" (bi) in "bi-man dalla" and in "bi-manih-tada" serves to make the two attributes of "a'lam" (most knowing) transitive, and it denotes association (mulabasah). That is, He is more knowing, associated with those who have strayed from His way, meaning associated with the state of this situation. As for the mention of those who are guided, it is a completion.

[Page 120]

It is connected to His saying, "Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way" (Qur'an 53:30), etc. Having stated that to God belong the affairs of both abodes through His saying, "To Him belong the Hereafter and the first [life]" (Qur'an 53:25), He moved on to the most important of what occurs in both abodes concerning the states of people, who are the noblest of what is on earth, in connection with His saying, "Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way" (Qur'an 53:30). What is meant by it is an indication of the recompense, and it is an affirmation of the occurrence of the Resurrection and the recompense.

The principal purpose of this speech is His saying "what is on the earth," because what matters is what is on the earth, since they are the object of recompense. "What is in the heavens" was mentioned along with it by way of completion (al-tatmim), to inform that God's dominion encompasses all that the worlds contain. The reason for beginning with the completion, rather than postponing it as the apparent rule for completions requires, is attention to the higher world, because it is broader and nobler; and so that the intended matter, which is His saying "that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did" (Qur'an 53:31) and what follows, is connected with what suits it of mention of what is on the earth, because those who are recompensed are the people of the earth. This is the reason for departing from what the apparent rule requires.

Thus it is permissible for His saying "that He may recompense" (li-yajziya) to be connected with the sense of "being" implied in the prepositional phrase that is the predicate about "what is in the heavens and what is on the earth." That is: existing as God's possession, with a cause that He may recompense those who did evil and those who did good from among the people of the earth, who are the ones from whom evil and good proceed. Thus the lam in His saying "li-yajziya" is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil); recompense is made the cause of the established fact of God's ownership of what is in the heavens and on the earth.

The meaning of this causation is that among the realities linked to the establishment of that ownership is a primary connection in conception and consideration, not in bringing into being. God's ownership of what is in the heavens and on earth results from God's bringing those creatures into existence, and God, when He brought them into existence, knew that they have two lives, and that they have good and bad deeds in the life of this world, and He knows that He will recompense them for their deeds according to what suits them, an everlasting recompense in the Hereafter. Therefore recompense was certainly the end-purpose of bringing into existence those on the earth, and so it is regarded as the cause of their creation. It is a motivating cause (ʿilla bāʿitha), which may allow other causes to accompany it, because the multiplicity of motivating causes lies within wisdom.

It is also permissible for it to be connected with "is most knowing" (a'lam) in His saying "He is most knowing of who strays from His way" (Qur'an 53:30). That is: among the special features of His knowledge, which nothing escapes, is that His knowledge is the basis for the recompense.

The preposition "bi" in His saying "for what they did" and His saying "with the best" serves to make the verb "yajziya" and "yajziya" transitive; so what follows the two prepositions has the sense of the object of the two verbs, and they are attached to the recompense. His saying "for what they did" then has the implied sense "with the like of what they did," that is, a just recompense equal to what they did. Therefore it is treated as being in the position of the very thing they did, following the manner of eloquent comparison (al-tashbih al-baligh).

As for His saying "with the best," that is, "with the good reward," that is, "with what is better than what they did." It contains an indication of the multiplication of good deeds, like His saying "Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it" (Qur'an 27:89). "Al-husna" is an adjective of an implied noun indicated by "yajziya," and it is the reward (al-mathuba) in the sense of recompense (al-thawab).

The order of the detailed statement of the recompense for the evildoers and the good-doers follows the order of its summary in His saying "Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided" (Qur'an 53:30), in the manner of the arrangement of folding and unfolding (al-laff wa al-nashr al-murattab).

His saying "those who avoid the major sins of wrongdoing" (Qur'an 53:32) etc. is an adjective of "those who did good," that is: those who did good and avoided the major sins of wrongdoing and the indecencies (al-fawahish), that is: they did good deeds and avoided what is forbidden, and that comprises piety (al-taqwa). This is an alert that avoiding what was mentioned is considered part of doing good, because committing evil deeds is incompatible with describing them as "those who did good." If they perform all good deeds but do not abandon evil deeds, their committing evil deeds is not doing good; and if they abandon evil deeds but also abandon good deeds, their abandoning good deeds is an evil.

The majority recited "kaba'ira al-ithm" in the plural form of "kabira" (major). Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "kabira al-ithm" in the singular masculine form, because a noun of genus is the same whether singular or plural.

What is meant by "kaba'ir al-ithm" is the great sins in what God legislated, which are those that the religion has emphatically warned against, or that it mentioned with a threat of punishment, or that it prescribed a specific penalty (hadd) for their perpetrator.

Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) said: "The major sins are every transgression that indicates little concern on the part of its perpetrator for religion and weakness in his adherence to it."

The conjunction of "al-fawahish" implies that what is joined to it is distinct from the major sins, but the distinction is one of partial overlap in generality and specificity: the indecencies are more specific than the major sins, and they are greater in sinfulness.

"Al-fawahish" are the acts for which the one who commits them is regarded as exceeding the major sins, such as fornication, theft, and assassination by stealth (qatl al-ghilah). This has been discussed earlier in the commentary on Surah al-An'am at His saying "Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden" (Qur'an 7:33) and what follows, and in Surah al-Nisa' at His saying "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden" (Qur'an 4:31).

The exception of "al-lamam" is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), because "al-lamam" is neither among the major sins of wrongdoing nor among the indecencies. So the exception has the sense of a corrective addition (al-istidrak). Its rationale is that what is called "al-lamam" is a kind of disobedience warned against in the religion, and people might think that the prohibition of it puts it in the category of major sins; therefore the corrective addition is appropriate. The benefit of this corrective addition is general and specific. As for the general benefit: so that Muslims do not treat the one who commits any of it in the manner of one who commits major sins. As for the specific benefit: it is mercy toward the Muslims who may commit it, so that its commission does not weaken the zeal of the Muslim in obedience and his attention is directed toward avoiding the major sins. This corrective addition is therefore good news for them, and the meaning is not that God permitted the committing of "al-lamam." Wadhdhah al-Yaman erred in his saying, which arose from misunderstanding of the Book of God and meddling in what is not his craft:

"She did not yield until I humbled myself before her, and I informed her of what God permitted in al-lamam."

"Al-lamam" is a forbidden act that falls short of the major sins and the indecencies in the severity of its prohibition, and it is that which people rarely abandon, so that it is sufficient from them to avoid frequent commission of it. This category is called "the minor sins" (al-saghair) by the scholars of the Shari'ah, in contrast to the naming of the other category.

They have illustrated "al-lamam" in forbidden desires by a kiss and a glance. It is named "al-lamam," which is the verbal noun of "alamma bi-l-makan" (to visit a place), meaning to stop there briefly without staying long. From the verses of the Book:

"My feathers are from you, and my passion is with you, even if your visits are only brief (lamam)."

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning a man named Nabhan al-Tammar, who had a shop in which he sold dates, in Medina. A woman came to buy dates, and he said to her: "What is inside the shop is better than this." When she entered, he solicited her, but she refused. He regretted this and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "There is nothing a man does except that I have done it," meaning by force against her, "except intercourse." Then this verse was revealed. That is, this verse would then be Medinan, appended to the Meccan Surah al-Najm, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

The meaning is: God overlooked it for his repentance. Some exegetes interpreted "al-lamam" as resolving to commit an evil deed without doing it, which would be a figurative visiting (ilmam majazi).

His saying "Indeed, your Lord is of vast forgiveness" (Qur'an 53:32) is a justification for the exception of "al-lamam" from their avoiding the major sins of wrongdoing and the indecencies, as a condition for the establishment of the attribute of "those who did good" for them.

In the construction of the predication on making "your Lord" the subject rather than the proper name, there is an indication that vast forgiveness is gentleness toward His righteous servants, as is the manner of a Lord with His rightly-owned creature.

[Page 123]

In the attribution of "Lord" to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ) rather than the pronoun of the community, there is an allusion that this care for the good-doers among his community has come to them through his blessing.

"Al-wasi'" means one who forgives much. Breadth (al-si'ah) is borrowed for abundance of encompassing, because a spacious place can contain a large number of people who dwell in it. God the Exalted said: "Our Lord, You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge" (Qur'an 40:7), and it has been discussed in Surah Ghafir.

* * *

"He is most knowing of you when He brought you forth from the earth, and when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers. So do not claim your own purity; He is most knowing of who fears Him" (Qur'an 53:32).

The address is to the believers. Its occurrence right after His saying "that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did and recompense those who did good with the best" (Qur'an 53:31) indicates that its meaning is connected with the meaning of that. Therefore it is not directed at the Jews, as in the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) of al-Wahidi and others. Its origin is from Abdullah ibn Lahi'ah, from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews, when a young child of theirs died, would say: 'He is a truthful one (siddiq).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'The Jews have lied. No soul that God creates in its mother's womb is except that it is either wretched or blessed.'" Then God revealed this verse. Abdullah ibn Lahi'ah was weakened by Ibn Ma'in, and Waki', Yahya al-Qattan, and Ibn Mahdi abandoned him. Al-Dhahabi said: "The practice is to weaken him." I say: Perhaps one of the narrators of this hadith did not transmit it accurately when he said, "Then God revealed this verse." Rather, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it, taking it in the generality of His saying "He is most knowing of you when He brought you forth from the earth" etc., as an argument against them. Otherwise, the surah is Meccan, and the disputation with the Jews took place in Medina.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Tha'labi related from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that it was revealed concerning a group of believers who boasted of their deeds. It seems that the motive for seeking a cause of revelation is to show the connection of His saying "So do not claim your own purity" with what precedes and follows it, and that it completes the meaning of the breadth of forgiveness by showing the breadth of mercy and kindness toward His servants, since He dealt with them by the path of ease and lightening, so He pardoned what would have burdened them had He taken them to account for it. Thus His saying "He is most knowing of you" is like His saying "Now God has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you" (Qur'an 8:66) and what follows. Then the speech proceeds, as a derivation, with His saying "So do not claim your own purity."

Therefore the clause "He is most knowing of you" to its end should be taken as a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani) for the clause "Indeed your Lord is of vast forgiveness," because of the favor contained in the clause "Indeed your Lord is of vast forgiveness." It is as if the hearers, when they heard that favor, thanked God, and the thought of seeking the cause of this mercy toward them occurred to their minds. So they were answered that their Lord knows their state better than they themselves do, and He arranges for them what does not occur to their minds. A parallel to this is in the sacred hadith: God the Exalted said, "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, of good, far beyond what you have witnessed."

His saying "when He brought you forth" is a temporal clause (zarf) connected to "most knowing." That is: He is most knowing of people from the time He brought them forth from the earth, which is the time of the creation of their origin, Adam.

Its meaning: their being produced from the earth entails that their capacity to bear hardships is weak, along with the varying stages of the creation of the children of Adam. God knew this, and knew that the last of the nations, which is the nation of the Prophet (ﷺ), is the weakest of the nations. This meaning is what came in the hadith of the Night Journey, in the words of Musa to Muhammad, peace be upon them both, when God imposed fifty prayers upon his nation: "Your nation cannot bear that, and I have tested the Children of Israel," meaning that they were stronger than your nation. So the meaning is that the weakness that calls for broad overlooking through forgiveness has been decreed in God's knowledge from the time of Adam's creation from the earth, with the weakness inherent in the human species, varying in degree. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa: 28]. The creation of the origin of man from the earth, which is a weak element, entails that weakness is inseparable from all the individuals descended from that origin. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Woman was created from a crooked rib."

His saying ﴿And when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers﴾ pertains specifically to the breadth of forgiveness and gentleness toward this nation, and this is what is implied by His saying: ﴿God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

Ajinna (embryos) is the plural of janin (embryo), which is the offspring of an animal while it is in the womb; it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, because it is concealed in three darknesses.

Page 125

"In the wombs of your mothers" is a descriptive qualifier that clarifies, since janin is only applied to what is in its mother's womb.

The benefit of this clarification is that it contains a reminder of the varying stages of embryos from the time of conception until birth, and an indication of the comprehensive knowledge of God Most High of those stages.

The clause ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the clause ﴿He knows best who is pious among you﴾ and the clause ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away…﴾, and the fa' is for the consequence of the parenthetical insertion. It is a warning to the believers against self-admiration with their good deeds, an admiration that a person generates within himself, or that one person instills in another by praising him for his deed.

Tuzakku is the present tense of zakka, which is of the intensive form whose purpose is to attribute the object to the root of the verb, like jahhalahu, meaning: do not attribute purity (zakah) to yourselves.

So His saying "anfusakum" (yourselves) applies to a person's purifying himself, whether in private or in public. Thus the plural in "fa-la tuzakku" returns to the matching of plural with plural, which implies distribution over the individuals, like: "the people mounted their animals."

The meaning: do not consider yourselves pure, and seek to increase nearness to God; or do not trust that you are pure, lest self-admiration enter you because of your deeds. This includes a person mentioning his good deeds to boast of them, or displaying them to people, and this is not permitted unless it brings about a general benefit, as Yusuf said: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾. From al-Kalbi and Muqatil: people used to do good deeds and then say: "our prayer, our fasting, our pilgrimage, and our struggle," so God Most High revealed this verse.

It also includes a person purifying another, so "anfusakum" returns to the sense of "your people" or "your community," like His saying: ﴿When you enter houses, greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61], meaning: let some of you greet others. The meaning: let none of you praise another for righteousness and obedience, lest that change him.

A prohibition has come in hadiths against purifying people by their deeds. Among them is the hadith of Umm 'Atiyyah when 'Uthman ibn Maz'un died in her house, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon him. Umm 'Atiyyah said: "May God's mercy be upon you, Abu al-Sa'ib" (the kunya of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un), "so my testimony about you is that God has honored you." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her: "And what makes you know that God has honored him?" She said: "If God does not honor him, who then will God honor?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "As for him, certainty has come to him, and I hope good for him. Yet by God, I do not know, though I am the Messenger of God, what will be done with me." Umm 'Atiyyah said: "So I will never purify anyone after hearing this from the Messenger of God" (ﷺ).

Among the etiquette of the era of prophethood that spread among the Companions was caution against purifying others, and they would say when praising someone: "I know nothing of him but good, and I do not vouch for anyone before God."

Muslim narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Amr and Ibn 'Ata', who said: "I named my daughter Barrah, and Zaynab bint Abi Salamah said to me: 'The Messenger of God forbade this name.' I was named Barrah, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Do not claim purity for yourselves, for God knows best who is righteous among you.' They said: 'What shall we name her?' He said: 'Name her Zaynab.'"

It has become clear that the prohibition is directed at a person saying anything that implies the purity of the soul, meaning its cleanness and righteousness, delegating that to God. For people's inner states differ from their outward appearances, and the gap between their kinds is wide. This is among the disciplines of caution in judgment and vigilance in assessment, and suspicion of indicators and superficial signs.

Thus this prohibition does not include reporting about people's conditions based on what is known of them and what has been tested in them of trustworthiness and integrity in testimony and transmission. Tazkiyah may be used to mean ta'dil (certifying reliability), and this is a term that is not intended in the same sense as His saying ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾; rather, it is a term that people agreed upon after the revelation of the Qur'an, and its intended meaning is clear.

The clause ﴿He knows best who is pious﴾ occurs as an explanation of the reason for the prohibition, or of its most important reasons. That is: entrust that matter to God, for He knows best who is pious, that is, the state of the one who is pious, whether in the perfection of piety, its deficiency, or its counterfeiting. This is the meaning of what came in the hadith: whoever reports about someone with good should say, "I do not vouch for anyone before God," that is, I do not purify anyone who presumes upon God's right, meaning, one who exceeds my measure.

[p. 127]

﴿Have you considered the one who turned away, and gave a little and then withheld?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾

The fa' (الفاء) here introduces a consequence to the amazed interrogative, following His words: ﴿That He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did, and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. This is because the state of this one who turned away, gave a little and withheld, is one of ignorance that for man is only what he strove for. What happened at the time of the revelation of the preceding verse, or before it, was an incident that revealed a misunderstanding of God's intent from His servants, although it is clear to whoever applies the right understanding. So, on the basis of all this, an amazement at the deviation of their understandings is made.

The one who turned away and gave a little is here not a group like the one meant by His words: ﴿So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance﴾ [al-Najm: 29]; rather he is a specific individual. The exegetes and transmitters agree that what is meant here is a specific person, and perhaps this is the reason for expressing him with the word (الَّذِي) rather than (مَن), because (الَّذِي) is more apparent in referring to a single specific person than the word (مَن).

They differed about identifying this one who turned away and gave a little. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi related from Mujahid and Ibn Zayd that what is meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. They said: "He used to sit with the Prophet ﷺ and listen to his recitation, and the Messenger of God ﷺ would admonish him. He came close to becoming Muslim, but a man from the polytheists (whose name they did not mention) rebuked him and said: 'Why did you abandon the religion of the elders and mislead them, and claim that they are in the Fire? You should have supported them. How will your fathers be treated?' He said: 'I feared the punishment of God.' The man said: 'Give me something, and I will bear for you all the punishment that is upon you.' So he gave him something." (Perhaps that was among them a binding commitment that binds the one who undertakes it, and they did not believe in the recompense of the Hereafter; so perhaps he sought to escape the anger of God in this world and returned to polytheism.) When he asked him for more, he held back and was stingy, and withheld.

Al-Qurtubi related from al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, and from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, and from al-Dahhak that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

It occurs in the asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation, i.e. the circumstances of revelation) of al-Wahidi and in al-Kashshaf that it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, when he prevented Uthman ibn Affan from spending on a good cause that he used to spend, that is, before Abdullah ibn Sa'd became Muslim. Al-Tha'labi related it from a group [of people]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "That is false, and Uthman is too exalted for such a thing," meaning: [it is false that] he would give ear to Ibn Abi Sarh regarding what he prevented him from.

[p. 128]

So His words, Exalted is He, ﴿the one who turned away﴾ indicate that he turned away from considering Islam after he had come close to it. His words ﴿and gave a little and withheld﴾ indicate what he gave to the one who would bear the punishment on his behalf.

The description of him with "turned away" (تَوَلّى) is not included within the amazement, but it is brought in the manner of blame. His giving is described as "little" as a preparation for blaming him: that, despite the smallness of what he gave, he was stingy with it and cut it off. His words "and withheld" (وأكْدى) indicate his stinginess and his cutting off of giving. It is said: akdā al-ladhi yahfuru (he who digs became stuck) when he encounters a kudya, that is, a rock he cannot remove. This is a second blame for stinginess, in addition to his remoteness from steadfastness in disbelief. So the amazement arises from the whole condition of al-Walid, to belittle his intellect and the weakness of his opinion. It is also said that what is meant by His words "and gave a little" is that he gave to the one whose acceptance and inclination toward Islam was small; and "and withheld" means he ceased after he had come close, as the digger of a well stops when a kudya obstructs him.

The interrogative in (أعِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ الغَيْبِ) is denunciatory (إنكاري), rejecting his supposition that hiring someone to bear God's punishment on his behalf saves him from the punishment; that is, "there is not with him knowledge of the unseen." This statement is a kinaya (metaphor by implication) for his error in what he imagined.

The sentence is an istinaf bayani (explanatory resumptive clause, a sentence that answers an implied question) for the amazed interrogative in His words ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away...﴾ and so on.

The fronting of (عِنْدَهُ), which is predicate, over (عِلْمُ الغَيْبِ), which is subject, is for emphasis on this strange claim of "with-ness" (ʿindiyya), and it indicates his distance from this rank.

"Knowledge of the unseen" is knowing the hidden worlds, that is, knowledge obtained from proofs; it is as if he had witnessed the unseen, by the indication of His words ﴿so that he sees﴾.

He made His words ﴿so that he sees﴾ a consequence of this amazement, that is, so that he witnesses the matters of the unseen, in such a way that he has concluded a contract regarding the conflict over its rights. The seeing in His words ﴿so that he sees﴾ is visual (بَصَرِيَّة), and its object is omitted; the estimated meaning is: "so that he sees the unseen."

[p. 129]

The meaning is: he secured himself from the consequence of turning away from Islam by paying something to the one who bears the consequence of his turning away, as if he knew the unseen and witnessed that this averts punishment from him. His action was thus "a bundle of grass on top of a heavy load" (ضِغْثًا عَلى إبالَةٍ), because he thought that turning away was a crime, and he paid the wealth only because he imagined that crimes can be assumed by another in the Hereafter.

The fronting of the pronoun, which is the subject, before its verb, rather than saying "fa-yara," is for the purpose of strengthening the judgment, like the example: "he gives abundantly" (هو يُعْطِي الجَزِيلَ). This strengthening is based on his manifest certainty in the transaction he contracted, and it is more fitting for the amazement at his condition.

[p. 127]

﴿Have you considered the one who turned away, and gave a little and then withheld?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾

The fa' (الفاء) here introduces a consequence to the amazed interrogative, following His words: ﴿That He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did, and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. This is because the state of this one who turned away, gave a little and withheld, is one of ignorance that for man is only what he strove for. What happened at the time of the revelation of the preceding verse, or before it, was an incident that revealed a misunderstanding of God's intent from His servants, although it is clear to whoever applies the right understanding.
