**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 36–38:**

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Moses﴾ ﴿and Abraham, who fulfilled [his trust]﴾ ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

"Am" (أم) here is for the idrab (إضراب, a turning away from one matter to another; in grammar, a shift of topic). It shifts from a matter that is astonishing and rejected to another that is equally rejected: his ignorance of what those who fear God should know from the knowledge of what came through the tongues of the earlier messengers. If he does not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), then why does he not seek what the messengers before him reported? He and his people have often mentioned their names and their laws in general, and he and his people have often asked the People of the Book about the reports concerning Moses. So why does he not ask about what was transmitted concerning them on this matter, which he strives for, namely seeking salvation from the punishment of God, so that those who act upon it may inform him? The distinguished features of Abraham's law are partly transmitted among the Arabs, and the law of Moses is known among the Jews. Thus the interrogative implied after "am" is a rejection, like the interrogative mentioned before it in God's words ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen?﴾ [al-Najm: 35]. The implied sense is: "Rather, has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Moses, etc."

The scrolls of Moses are the Torah. The scrolls of Abraham are scrolls in which he recorded what God revealed to him, and they are the ones mentioned in surah al-A'la: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 18]. Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim transmitted from Abu Dhar that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the books that were sent down to the prophets, and he mentioned to him ten scrolls sent down to Abraham, meaning: what is written in them was sent down to him.

The reason the scrolls of Abraham are singled out for mention is that the Arabs know Abraham and his law, and they call it the Hanifiyya (الحنيفية, the upright monotheistic religion). Some of them may have claimed to have some knowledge of it, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.

As for the scrolls of Moses, they are well known among the People of the Book, and the Arabs mix with the Jews in Khaybar, Qurayza, al-Nadir and Taymaa, and mix with the Christians of Najran. God the Exalted has said: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 48].

The scrolls of Moses are mentioned first because they are renowned for the abundance of guidance and law they contain, whereas of the scrolls of Abraham only a few things were transmitted. They are estimated at ten scrolls, meaning the quantity of ten pages in the ancient script, each page holding about four verses of the Qur'an, so that the total of what is in the scrolls of Abraham amounts to about forty verses.

In surah al-A'la the scrolls of Abraham were mentioned before the scrolls of Moses, in consideration of their being substitutes for the former scrolls, so the earlier of the two was mentioned first.

In my view, the scrolls of Abraham are placed later here so that what follows contains, in summary, what the scrolls of Abraham comprise. Thus the scrolls of Abraham are the "words" with which God tested Abraham, mentioned in His words in surah al-Baqara: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], meaning he conveyed them to his people and to those who believed in him. His words here "who fulfilled" carry the meaning of His words "and he fulfilled them" in surah al-Baqara.

The description of Abraham with this is a testimony against the polytheists that Abraham conveyed what was revealed to him to his people and his offspring, but the Arabs neglected that and replaced the Hanifiyya with polytheism.

The object of "fulfilled" is omitted so that it encompasses many kinds of fulfilment, among them what is in God's words ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and what is in His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105].

God's words ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ may be a substitution (badal) for "mā" in "what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham." It is a detailed substitution from a general one, and "an" (أن) is then the lightened form of the heavy "inna." The implied sense is: "Has he not been informed that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another?"

It is also possible that "an" is explanatory (tafsiriyya), explaining what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham, because what is in the scrolls is something written, and writing in them carries the meaning of speech without its letters. So what is in the scrolls of Moses is fit to be explained by the explanatory "an." Al-Qurtubi, in his tafsir of God's words in this surah ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56], transmitted from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, who said: "These are the words that God mentioned from His words ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham﴾ up to His words ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]; all of this is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."

"Tazir" (تزر) is the imperfect of wazara, when one commits a burden (wizr, sin). The feminine form of "wazira" is by way of interpretation as "soul" (nafs), and likewise the feminine of "ukhra." The occurrence of "nafs" and "ukhra" in a negative context conveys generality, so it includes the rejection of what al-Walid ibn al-Mughira claimed, namely that a man would bear the punishment of God on his behalf.

This is among what was in the scrolls of Abraham, and among it is what God related in His words ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 87], ﴿the Day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 88], ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 89].

It is related in the Torah from Abraham that he said, concerning the people of Lot: "Will You destroy the righteous along with the wicked?"

As for its parallel in the scrolls of Moses, in the Torah: "Fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor children put to death for the fathers; every person shall be put to death for his own sin." God related of Moses his words ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The general wording of "wizr" requires that the ruling applies universally to matters of this world and matters of the Hereafter.

As for His words in the Torah that God said: "I will visit the children for the iniquities of the fathers, to the third generation," this concerns the ordering of effects upon worldly causes, and it is a warning.

Bearing the burden of another, for one who is the cause of another's sin, is not an additional burden over his own sin in the manner of bearing another's burden; rather it is of the kind of an increase in punishment because of misleading others. God the Exalted said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. In a hadith: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing."

God the Exalted has said: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 48].

The scrolls of Moses are mentioned first because they are renowned for the abundance of guidance and law they contain, whereas of the scrolls of Abraham only a few things were transmitted. They are estimated at ten scrolls, meaning the quantity of ten pages in the ancient script, each page holding about four verses of the Qur'an, so that the total of what is in the scrolls of Abraham amounts to about forty verses.

In surah al-A'la the scrolls of Abraham were mentioned before the scrolls of Moses, in consideration of their being substitutes for the former scrolls, so the earlier of the two was mentioned first.

In my view, the scrolls of Abraham are placed later here so that what follows contains, in summary, what the scrolls of Abraham comprise. Thus the scrolls of Abraham are the "words" with which God tested Abraham, mentioned in His words in surah al-Baqara: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], meaning he conveyed them to his people and to those who believed in him. His words here "who fulfilled" carry the meaning of His words "and he fulfilled them" in surah al-Baqara.

The description of Abraham with this is a testimony against the polytheists that Abraham conveyed what was revealed to him to his people and his offspring, but the Arabs neglected that and replaced the Hanifiyya with polytheism.

The object of "fulfilled" is omitted so that it encompasses many kinds of fulfilment, among them what is in God's words ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and what is in His words ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105].

God's words ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ may be a substitution (badal) for "mā" in "what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham." It is a detailed substitution from a general one, and "an" (أن) is then the lightened form of the heavy "inna." The implied sense is: "Has he not been informed that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another?"

It is also possible that "an" is explanatory (tafsiriyya), explaining what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham, because what is in the scrolls is something written, and writing in them carries the meaning of speech without its letters. So what is in the scrolls of Moses is fit to be explained by the explanatory "an." Al-Qurtubi, in his tafsir of God's words in this surah ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56], transmitted from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, who said: "These are the words that God mentioned from His words ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham﴾ up to His words ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]; all of this is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."

"Tazir" (تزر) is the imperfect of wazara, when one commits a burden (wizr, sin). The feminine form of "wazira" is by way of interpretation as "soul" (nafs), and likewise the feminine of "ukhra." The occurrence of "nafs" and "ukhra" in a negative context conveys generality, so it includes the rejection of what al-Walid ibn al-Mughira claimed, namely that a man would bear the punishment of God on his behalf.

This is among what was in the scrolls of Abraham, and among it is what God related in His words ﴿and do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 87], ﴿the Day when neither wealth nor children will avail﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 88], ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 89].

It is related in the Torah from Abraham that he said, concerning the people of Lot: "Will You destroy the righteous along with the wicked?"

As for its parallel in the scrolls of Moses, in the Torah: "Fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor children put to death for the fathers; every person shall be put to death for his own sin." God related of Moses his words ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The general wording of "wizr" requires that the ruling applies universally to matters of this world and matters of the Hereafter.

As for His words in the Torah that God said: "I will visit the children for the iniquities of the fathers, to the third generation," this concerns the ordering of effects upon worldly causes, and it is a warning.

Bearing the burden of another, for one who is the cause of another's sin, is not an additional burden over his own sin in the manner of bearing another's burden; rather it is of the kind of an increase in punishment because of misleading others. God the Exalted said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. In a hadith: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 39 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And that man has only what he strives for.﴾

It is coordinated with the clause "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (al-Najm 38), so it may be coordinated with the preposition-governed noun in "bi-" (in "bima fi suhuf Musa"), in which case "an" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna"; or it may be coordinated with "alla tazir wazira wizra ukhra," in which case "an" is explanatory (tafsiriyya). On both possibilities, "an" is an emphatic restatement of its counterpart in the clause it is coordinated with.

The definite article in "al-insan" is the generic definite (ta'rif al-jins). Its occurrence in a context of negation conveys generality. The meaning: nothing belongs to him except what he himself strove for.

Al-sa'y means work and acquisition. Its original sense is walking, and it was applied to work by way of metonymy (majaz mursal) or allusion (kinaya). Here it means the doing of good, as indicated by the mention of the particle of possession (lam al-ikhtisas) and by its being set in contrast to the words "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (al-Najm 38).

The meaning: no one gains the benefit of an action except what he himself did, so there is no benefit for him from the action of another. The lam of possession indicates that what is meant is the righteous deeds he strove for. Accordingly, this statement completes the meaning of "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (al-Najm 38), as a safeguard lest it occur to the mind that the removal of burden from one who did not commit it means that the good may reach one who did not perform it.

The meaning of the verse is related in the Qur'an from Abraham in his words: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 89).

This verse is a report about the law (shar') of Abraham and Moses. Since it is established that the law of those before us is law for us as long as no abrogating text has come, this verse indicates that the work of one person does not suffice for another, whether obligatory or voluntary, in the case of individual obligation (fard 'ayn). As for one person assuming a financial liability for an act done by another, such as the blood-money (diya) for accidental killing, that falls under the obligatory mutual support.

The scholars differed in interpreting this verse and its scope. From 'Ikrima it is reported that the words of the Exalted ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾ are a report about a previous law, and so do not bind in our law. He means that the law of Islam abrogated that, so that the acceptance of one person's work on behalf of another is among the distinctive features of this community.

From al-Rabi' ibn Anas it is reported that he interpreted "man" (al-insan) in the words of the Exalted ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾ as the disbelieving man; as for the believer, he has his own striving and what others strive on his behalf.

Among the scholars is one who interpreted the verse as negating that a person should have the benefit of what another did, if the one who strove did not make his work for another. It seems this inclines toward the view that the use of "sa'a" in the verse is one of the use of a term in its literal and its figurative (intellectual) senses. Ibn al-Faras relates that among the scholars is one who took the verse according to its apparent meaning, that no one benefits from another's work. It is understood from Ibn al-Faras's words that among those who said so was al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, regarding the validity of a hire for performing the pilgrimage.

Know that the evidences for the reaching of the reward of some deeds to someone other than the one who did them are established in general, and views differ only regarding detail or generalization. The Exalted said: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join their offspring with them and will not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾ (al-Tur 21), and we have explained this in the commentary on surah al-Tur. And He said: ﴿Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted﴾ (al-Zukhruf 70), so He made the spouses of the righteous believing women and the spouses of the righteous believing women and men enjoy Paradise together, although disparity among spouses in deeds is necessary; and we have explained this in the commentary on surah al-Zukhruf.

In the Sahih of Muslim: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except from three: ongoing charity (sadaqa jariya), or knowledge from which benefit is derived, or a righteous child who prays for him." It is general in respect of everything a person does, and the criterion of its generality is the exception; the exception is evidence that the three excepted things are from the person's own work. 'Iyad said in al-Ikmal: since he was the cause of these things, they are from his acquisition. I say: this is evident regarding ongoing charity and knowledge he disseminated; as for the prayer of a righteous child for one of his parents, al-Nawawi said: because the child is from his acquisition. Al-Ubbi said: the hadith "a man's child is from his acquisition" makes the exception of these three a connected (muttasil) exception.

Sound reports have been established from the Prophet ﷺ indicating that one person's work on behalf of another suffices for the one on whose behalf it is done. In the Muwatta' is the hadith of al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas that a woman from Khath'am asked the Messenger of God ﷺ, saying: "The obligation of God upon His servants regarding the pilgrimage has reached my father, who is an old man who cannot stay on the mount; may I perform the pilgrimage on his behalf?" He said: "Yes, perform the pilgrimage on his behalf." In her saying "who cannot stay on the mount" there is an indication that her pilgrimage on his behalf was voluntary.

In the Book of Abu Dawud is the hadith of Buraydah that a woman came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "My mother has died and owes a month of fasting; will it suffice, or may I fast on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." She said: "And she did not perform the pilgrimage; will it suffice, or may I perform it on her behalf?" He said: "Yes."

In the same book is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that a man said: "O Messenger of God, my mother has died; will it benefit her if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes."

In the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-'As, when his brother Hisham had freed slaves on behalf of their father al-'As ibn Wa'il, 'Amr asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about doing the same as his brother had done. He said to him: "If your father had been a Muslim, and you freed on his behalf, or gave charity on his behalf, or performed the pilgrimage on his behalf, it would have reached him."

It is related that 'A'isha freed slaves on behalf of her brother 'Abd al-Rahman after his death and observed i'tikaf on his behalf.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, that they issued a fatwa regarding a woman whose mother had vowed on herself a prayer at the mosque of Quba' and did not fulfil her vow: that she should pray on her behalf at the mosque of Quba'.

"The Prophet ﷺ commanded Sa'd ibn 'Ubada to fulfil a vow his mother had made." It was said it was a manumission, and it was said it was charity, and it was said it was an unrestricted vow.

This verse and the reports that are established have been a field for the scholars' views regarding reconciling the two, adhering to the apparent meaning of the verse, and restricting the matter to the kind of act for which the Prophet ﷺ gave permission, or analogizing upon it.

It is necessary to note first that obligatory duties, whether fard or sunnah, which are required of the individual, have as their purpose, in demanding them from the responsible person, what is achieved through them of purifying his soul so that he becomes a righteous part. So if another performs them on his behalf, the purpose of addressing each Muslim with them is lost. Likewise, abstention from prohibited things does not admit of substitution, because abstention does not admit of repetition. So in this category, a person has only what he strives for, and the substitution of another in its performance is not valid. As for faith, its matter is clear: the reality of faith does not admit of multiplicity such that one believes for himself and believes on behalf of another; for when one holds a firm conviction, that becomes his faith. Ibn al-Faras said in Ahkam al-Qur'an: they agreed that no one believes on behalf of anyone.

As for what is other than faith among the obligatory laws of Islam, what is among them of bodily acts, a person has only what he strives for, and the striving of another does not suffice for him; because the purpose of the individually required matters, which a person must perform himself, is what they contain of purifying the soul and training it toward good, as has preceded just now.

Similar to this are the regular supererogatory prayers and acts of worship, so that a person may become righteous and be trained in watchfulness of his Lord in his heart and deed and submission to Him, the Exalted, so that through the righteousness of individuals the righteousness of the whole community may be realized; and substitution defeats this meaning.

So whatever is among acts of good not specifically required, such as voluntary acts of worship, has two purposes: a purpose attached to the purpose found in specifically required acts, and the purpose of increasing good in the community of Muslims through righteous deeds and words; and this second consideration is not defeated by substitution.

I do not see the distinction between what is a person's act with his body and what is his act with his wealth as an influential distinction in this matter. The sound view is that the rule applies uniformly to both types, whether by admitting substitution or by not admitting it: charities, fasting, voluntary prayers, and equipping fighters for jihad that is not obligatory on the Muslim who equips or on the one who is equipped, and the righteous words in the recitation of the Qur'an, glorification, praise and the like, and prayer upon the Prophet ﷺ. By this, the locus of the disagreement Ibn al-Faras mentioned regarding the transfer of one person's act to another is clarified.

Al-Nawawi said: supplication reaches the reward to the deceased, and likewise charity, and both are agreed upon. Likewise the paying of debt. End of quote. Ibn al-Faras related the same, and the disagreement among the scholars of Islam concerns what is beyond that.

Malik said: one may perform voluntary acts on behalf of the deceased: one gives charity on his behalf, or frees on his behalf, or gifts on his behalf. As for those obligatory acts of worship composed of bodily work and the spending of wealth, such as pilgrimage, 'umra and jihad, al-Baji said: al-Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab related from the school that substitution is valid in them; and Ibn al-Qassar said: substitution is not valid in them. This is the well-known view of Malik. The basis of their disagreement is that Malik disliked that one should perform the pilgrimage on behalf of another; yet if he bequeathed it, his bequest is executed, and it does not discharge the obligation.

Al-Baji preferred the view of the validity of substitution in this, on the ground that Malik executed the bequest for it, and said: no one is hired for it except one who has performed the pilgrimage for himself, so a virgin (sarura, one who has never performed it) does not perform it on his behalf. Had the pilgrimage of the hired person not been on the basis of substitution for the one who bequeathed it, the attribute of the one who performs the pilgrimage would not have been taken into account. Ibn al-Faras said: Malik permitted the bequest of the obligatory pilgrimage, and held that if one bequeaths it, it is from his striving.

The reliable position of the Hanafi school is the validity of substitution in the pilgrimage for one who is unable, on condition that his incapacity continues until death; if his incapacity ends, the pilgrimage becomes obligatory upon him in person. Something other than this is sometimes transmitted from Abu Hanifa in the books of the Malikis.

Al-Shafi'i permitted performing the pilgrimage on behalf of the deceased and a deceased person's bequest of pilgrimage on his behalf. Ibn al-Faras said: in one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, it is not permitted, and he argued with the words of the Exalted: ﴿and that man has only what he strives for﴾. End of quote.

The school of Ahmad ibn Hanbal holds it permissible, and he is not obliged to repeat the pilgrimage if his excuse ends.

As for supererogatory acts other than obligatory ones and other than regular sunnah prayers, from all acts of righteousness and voluntary worship: as for performing the pilgrimage on behalf of one who is not able, al-Baji said: Ibn al-Jallab said in al-Tafri'": it is disliked to hire one who performs the pilgrimage on his behalf; if he did so, it is not annulled. Ibn al-Qassar said: "it is permitted in the case of the deceased, not the one incapacitated," meaning one unable to rise. Ibn Habib said: the concession has come regarding the elderly one who cannot rise, and regarding the deceased, that his son may perform the pilgrimage on his behalf even if he did not bequeath it.

Al-Ubbi said in his commentary on Muslim: it is mentioned that Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa, in the year he performed the pilgrimage, purchased a pilgrimage for the sultan Abu al-'Abbas al-Hafsi according to the view of one who differs, that is, contrary to the school of Malik.

As for prayer and fasting: Malik was asked about performing the pilgrimage on behalf of the deceased, and he said: as for prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage on his behalf, we do not hold that. In the Mudawwana he said: one performs voluntary acts on his behalf other than these; giving gifts on his behalf or freeing on his behalf is more beloved to me. Al-Baji said: he distinguished between these and expenditures.

Al-Shafi'i, in one of his opinions, said: the reward of voluntary prayers and all voluntary acts does not reach him. The author of al-Tawdih from the Shafi'is said: with us, substitution in voluntary pilgrimage is permitted according to the more correct of the two views. Ahmad said: it reaches him, the reward of prayers and all voluntary acts.

The well-known position of the school of al-Shafi'i is that the recitation of the Qur'an and gifting its reward to the deceased does not reach him as reward; Ahmad ibn Hanbal and many of al-Shafi'i's companions said that its reward reaches him.

Ibn al-Faras reported from the school of Malik that if someone recites the Qur'an and gives the reward of his recitation to a deceased person, that is permissible, and the deceased reaches its reward and benefit. Therefore, what is attributed to Malik about the impermissibility of gifting the reward of recitation in the books of those who disagree with him is not a verified position.

It has been narrated in the hadith of 'Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek protection for himself with the protective surahs (al-mu'awwidhat). When his illness grew severe, I would recite them over him and place his hand upon his body, hoping for their blessing." Is the recitation of the two protective surahs (al-mu'awwidhatayn) anything other than a substitution for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he used to do for himself? If substitution is valid in seeking protection and seeking blessing through the Qur'an, then why would it not be valid in the reward of recitation?

Page 138

Know that all of this concerns one person voluntarily performing an act of worship (qurba) on behalf of another. As for hiring someone to perform a substitute act of worship: regarding the Hajj, they have mentioned the permissibility of hiring someone, whether by bequest or otherwise, because spending is one of the constituents of the Hajj. It appears that every act of worship for which the doer may not take a wage for performing it, such as prayer and fasting, does not validly permit hiring someone to perform it as a substitute. And the acts of worship for which taking a wage is valid permit hiring someone to substitute in them, such as the recitation of the Qur'an. The Prophet (ﷺ) approved the action of those who took a wage for performing ruqyah (spiritual incantation) on one bitten by a scorpion or snake using the Opening Chapter of the Book (al-Fatiha).

When you know all of this, then His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾, is a ruling that was in an earlier law (shari'a). Those who say it does not apply to us find no contradiction between it and the reports, received in our religion, that establish the validity of substitution in acts. Those who hold that the law of those before us is law for us unless an abrogating (nasikh) text is revealed are of several kinds: some applied the general wording of the verse and interpreted the contrary reports as specific to the Prophet (ﷺ); some made those reports specifying the general wording (takhsis), or abrogating it; and some interpreted the apparent meaning of the verse as meaning that it does not grant a person that right in reality, such that he relies on his own deeds; or they interpreted "striving" (sa'y) as intention. And they interpreted the lam in His saying "for man" (lil-insan) as meaning "upon" (ʿala), or as meaning "he is not burdened with the sins of others."

In the commentary on Surah al-Rahman in al-Kashshaf (by al-Zamakhshari): 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir said to al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl: "Three verses have puzzled me." He mentioned among them His saying, ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾, so what about the multiplications, i.e., His saying, ﴿So that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾ [al-Baqara: 245]? Al-Husayn said: Its meaning is that he has nothing except what he strives for, as a matter of justice, and it is up to Me to reward him with one thing a thousandfold, as a matter of grace.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 53, verses 40–41:**

﴿And that his effort will be seen.﴾ ﴿Then he will be given the fullest reward.﴾

It is permissible for these words to be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, so that they form part of the explanation of what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim (ʿataf: coordination by conjunction). In that case, the change of style, namely the use of the emphatic particle *anna* (إنّ المشددة, the heavy form of "indeed/that"), is required by the context. The report concerns the human being's effort, that it will be made known on the Day of Resurrection. This follows from the principle that a person has only what he strove for. Since the word *saʿyahu* (سَعْيَهُ, "his effort") is suitable to be the noun of *anna*, the requirement for the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن) to be introduced falls away, and so the requirement for the light form *an* (أنِ المُخَفَّفَةِ) falls away as well. The content of this clause may also be, in the law of Ibrahim, what Allah related from him in his saying: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 87].

It is also permissible that the content of his saying *wa anna saʿyahu* (وأنَّ سَعْيَهُ) is not included in what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim. Then its conjunction with *mā* (ما), the relative pronoun in his saying ﴿with what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim﴾ [An-Najm: 36], is a conjunction of a single noun with a single noun. It would then be the object of the preposition (بـ) in his saying *fī ṣuḥuf Musa* (في صُحُفِ مُوسى), and so on. The sense is: he has not been informed that the effort of a human being will be seen, that is, that it will necessarily be seen, meaning that he will be recompensed for it. That is, he has not been informed of this religious truth. On this reading we do not need to seek the establishment of this clause's content in the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

*Sawfa* (سَوْفَ) is a particle of the future, and it is most common for it to refer to a distant future.

The meaning of *yurā* (يُرى, "will be seen"): it will be witnessed at the reckoning, as in Allah's saying ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ [Al-Kahf: 49]. It is therefore possible that deeds are embodied so that they become something witnessed. The matters of the Hereafter differ from the customary matters of this world. It is also possible that they are made into signs upon the deeds, by which the deeds are made known, as in Allah's saying ﴿Their light will run before them and on their right hands﴾ [At-Tahrim: 8]. And what is in the hadith: "For every treacherous person a banner will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'This is the treachery of so-and-so.'" Here a noun has been omitted by way of estimation, and the estimate is: *wa anna ʿunwāna saʿyihi sawfa yurā* (and that the heading/record of his effort will be seen).

It is also possible that this is by publicizing the deed and the effort, as in Allah's saying ﴿Are these the ones about whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? Enter Paradise﴾ [Al-A'raf: 49], to the end of the verse. And as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever makes his brother's faults known in what he dislikes, Allah will make him known to the hearers of His creation on the Day of Resurrection." In that case the sight (رؤية, *ru'yah*) is used figuratively for knowledge, with the aim of establishing knowledge and publicizing it.

The wisdom in this is the honouring of the good-doers with a good reputation and the humbling of the wrongdoers through a bad report.

His saying ﴿Then he will be given the fullest reward﴾ is the aim of the clause.

*Thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") here denotes a gradation of rank (التراخي الرتبي), because the attainment of the reward is more important than making it known, or than making known the one who is rewarded.

The pronoun of the object in his saying *yujzāhu* (يُجْزاهُ) refers to the effort, meaning: he is recompensed for it, or recompensed with it. The preposition was omitted and the word was put in the accusative by removing the preposition (نزع الخافض). It is very common to say *jazāhu ʿamaluhu* (جزاه عمله, "his deed recompensed him"), and its original form is *jazāhu ʿalā ʿamalihi* or *jazāhu bi-ʿamalihi*.

*Al-awfā* (الأوفى) is a superlative form (اسم تفضيل) from *al-wafāʾ*, which is completeness and perfection. The superlative is used here for intensity (في القوة), and it is not intended to compare it with anything else. The meaning is that the recompense for an act, whether good or evil, corresponds exactly to what was done. Allah said ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty﴾ [An-Nisa: 173]. He said ﴿And indeed We will pay them their share undiminished﴾ [Hud: 109]. He said ﴿And he found Allah with him, and He paid him his account in full﴾ [An-Nur: 39]. He said ﴿Indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense﴾ [Al-Isra: 63].

*Al-jazāʾ al-awfā* (الجزاءَ الأوفى) is in the accusative as an absolute object (المفعول المطلق) that specifies the type.

Allah has related about Ibrahim: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected.﴾

The content of this clause may also be, in the law of Ibrahim, what Allah related from him in his saying: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara: 87].

It is also permissible that the content of his saying *wa anna saʿyahu* (وأنَّ سَعْيَهُ) is not included in what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim. Then its conjunction with *mā* (ما), the relative pronoun in his saying ﴿with what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim﴾ [An-Najm: 36], is a conjunction of a single noun with a single noun. It would then be the object of the preposition (بـ) in his saying *fī ṣuḥuf Musa* (في صُحُفِ مُوسى), and so on. The sense is: he has not been informed that the effort of a human being will be seen, that is, that it will necessarily be seen, meaning that he will be recompensed for it. That is, he has not been informed of this religious truth. On this reading we do not need to seek the establishment of this clause's content in the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

*Sawfa* (سَوْفَ) is a particle of the future, and it is most common for it to refer to a distant future.

The meaning of *yurā* (يُرى, "will be seen"): it will be witnessed at the reckoning, as in Allah's saying ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ [Al-Kahf: 49]. It is therefore possible that deeds are embodied so that they become something witnessed. The matters of the Hereafter differ from the customary matters of this world. It is also possible that they are made into signs upon the deeds, by which the deeds are made known, as in Allah's saying ﴿Their light will run before them and on their right hands﴾ [At-Tahrim: 8]. And what is in the hadith: "For every treacherous person a banner will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'This is the treachery of so-and-so.'" Here a noun has been omitted by way of estimation, and the estimate is: *wa anna ʿunwāna saʿyihi sawfa yurā* (and that the heading/record of his effort will be seen).

It is also possible that this is by publicizing the deed and the effort, as in Allah's saying ﴿Are these the ones about whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? Enter Paradise﴾ [Al-A'raf: 49], to the end of the verse. And as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever makes his brother's faults known in what he dislikes, Allah will make him known to the hearers of His creation on the Day of Resurrection." In that case the sight (رؤية, *ru'yah*) is used figuratively for knowledge, with the aim of establishing knowledge and publicizing it.

The wisdom in this is the honouring of the good-doers with a good reputation and the humbling of the wrongdoers through a bad report.

His saying ﴿Then he will be given the fullest reward﴾ is the aim of the clause.

*Thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") here denotes a gradation of rank (التراخي الرتبي), because the attainment of the reward is more important than making it known, or than making known the one who is rewarded.

The pronoun of the object in his saying *yujzāhu* (يُجْزاهُ) refers to the effort, meaning: he is recompensed for it, or recompensed with it. The preposition was omitted and the word was put in the accusative by removing the preposition (نزع الخافض). It is very common to say *jazāhu ʿamaluhu* (جزاه عمله, "his deed recompensed him"), and its original form is *jazāhu ʿalā ʿamalihi* or *jazāhu bi-ʿamalihi*.

*Al-awfā* (الأوفى) is a superlative form (اسم تفضيل) from *al-wafāʾ*, which is completeness and perfection. The superlative is used here for intensity (في القوة), and it is not intended to compare it with anything else. The meaning is that the recompense for an act, whether good or evil, corresponds exactly to what was done. Allah said ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty﴾ [An-Nisa: 173]. He said ﴿And indeed We will pay them their share undiminished﴾ [Hud: 109]. He said ﴿And he found Allah with him, and He paid him his account in full﴾ [An-Nur: 39]. He said ﴿Indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense﴾ [Al-Isra: 63].

*Al-jazāʾ al-awfā* (الجزاءَ الأوفى) is in the accusative as an absolute object (المفعول المطلق) that specifies the type.

Allah has related about Ibrahim: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 42:

﴿And that to your Lord is the final destination.﴾

The discussion of its placement is the same as the discussion of the placement of the clause "and that his striving will be seen soon," so it is permissible that this clause be conjoined to the clause "and that his striving will be seen soon," making it a continuation of what is in the scriptures of Musa (Moses) and Ibrahim (Abraham). The address in His saying "to your Lord" would then be an iltifat (shift) from the third person to the second person, with the addressee unspecified, as if it had been said: "and that to his Lord is the final destination." Perhaps a parallel to it from the words of Ibrahim is what Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I will go to my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Saffat: 99].

It is also permissible that it is not among what the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim contained, and that its conjunction is the conjunction of a single noun to a single noun, so that the verbal noun formed from "anna" and its complement is governed by the preposition "bi" (in), meaning: he was not informed that to your Lord is the final destination. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ.

Page 141
Accordingly, we do not seek a parallel for it from the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

The meaning of "return to Allah" is the return to His pure judgment, which is not mixed with rulings that, outwardly, are among the dispositions of created beings, which are the affair of worldly matters. The speech is therefore elliptical, with an omitted modifier indicated by the context.

The expression of Allah by the word "your Lord" is an honouring of the Prophet ﷺ, and an allusive threat to those who denied him, because it is the nature of the Lord to defend His charge.

In the verse there is another meaning, namely that "the final destination" is a metaphor for the end of travel, in the sense of halting, since halting is the end of the traveller's journey. Halting is then a representation of the state of one who obeys Allah's command, likening Allah's command to that by which walls are bounded, after the manner of the saying of Abu al-Shish:

"Desire has brought me to a halt where you are, so there is no one behind it for me, nor anyone ahead of it."

Likewise this meaning is expressed by halting at the limit in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. The meaning is a warning against opposing what Allah has commanded and forbidden.

In the verse there is a third meaning, namely the end of the indication of existing things to the existence and oneness of Allah. For the one who looks at created beings knows that their existence is possible, not necessary, so they must have an originator. Then, if the whisperings of doubt suggest to the observer that he should posit for created beings an originator from among what appears to him, such as the sun, the moon, or fire, because of the great efficacy he sees in them, it will not be long before it becomes clear to him that that supposed thing is not free of change, which indicates its origination, so it must have a originator who brought it into being. Then, when imagination goes on to chain together supposed deities, as in the story of Ibrahim, when night covered him and he saw a star, he said, "This is my Lord"... the signs, reason finds no alternative but to arrive at the necessity of the existence of a Creator of all possible things, whose existence is not possible but necessary, and who is characterized by the attributes of perfection, and He is the true God. Thus Allah is the final destination at which the reasoning of the intellect ends. Then, when the proof of the existence of the Creator shines forth for him and leads him to establish that He is one, because if there were many, each of the many would not be of perfect divinity, since none of the many could dispose of what the other had disposed of; so each one would be in need of the other to be content with his acquiescence in what he had brought into being, and otherwise he would be able to annul what the other had done, so each of the many would necessarily need someone who permits him to exercise disposal. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nor was there with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have exalted themselves over others.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91] And He said: "Say: If there were with Him gods, as you say, then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne." And He said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. So the intellect inevitably arrives at a final destination.

﴿وأنَّهُ هو أضْحَكَ وأبْكى﴾.

This is a transition from reflection on the conditions of the Hereafter to reflection on the conditions of this world. The pronoun "huwa" (He) refers to your Lord, from His saying ﴿وأنَّ إلى رَبِّكَ المُنْتَهى﴾ [An-Najm: 42].

Laughter (ḍaḥk) is the effect of the soul's joy, and weeping (bukā') is the effect of sorrow. Both laughter and weeping are among the distinctive attributes of humankind, and both are a wondrous creation that indicates a great emotional state within the soul.

Other animals have neither laughter nor weeping. What is reported of applying these terms to animals is figurative (takhayyul) or metaphorical (tashbih), like the saying of al-Nabigha:

*"The weeping of a dove calling Hadil, ringed, upon a branch, singing."*

A human being is never free of the two states of sorrow and joy. If he is not grieved and distressed, he is joyful, because God created joy and exhilaration as constant companions of a human being through the soundness of his temperament and his perception. When he is sound, his nerves are active, and this activity produces a measure of gladness in general, even though it varies in strength and intensity. Thus, the mention of laughter and weeping conveys a comprehensive account of human conditions in brief, alludes to the causes of joy and sorrow, reminds one of the Wise Creator, and indicates that God is the One who disposes of the human being. He created the causes of his joy and his distress, and inspired him to acquire these by what lies within his capacity, while He set a great limit of these beyond human capacity. No one who reflects doubts this. Within it is also guidance toward turning to the obedience of God and humbly beseeching Him, that He might decree for people the causes of joy and ward off from them the causes of sorrow.

Page 143

This matter is mentioned in this context because the complete recompense for people's striving is that some of it gives joy to one group and some of it causes grief to another.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, "huwa") conveys restriction (qaṣr) of the attribute of creating the causes of laughter and weeping to God, Exalted is He, in order to refute a partner in the disposal of affairs, and thereby the association in divinity is refuted. This is a restriction of rejection of a partner (qaṣr ifrād), because the intended meaning is the negation of the disposal of anyone other than God, Exalted is He. Although this restriction, in relation to reality itself, is a true restriction (qaṣr ḥaqīqī) to refute the belief that Time (al-dahr) disposes of affairs.

The attribution of causing laughter and weeping to God, Exalted is He, is because He is the Creator of the two powers of laughter and weeping in a human being, which is a wondrous creation, and because He is the Creator of the natures of existent things that bring about the causes of laughter and weeping, namely joy and sorrow.

The object of "aḍḥaka" (He made laugh) and "abkā" (He made weep) is not mentioned, because the purpose is the two verbs themselves and not their objects. The two verbs are treated as intransitive, meaning: He brought laughter and weeping into existence.

Since the purpose of this is to establish that God, Exalted is He, alone disposes of the human being, through what people find in the states of their own selves, namely that the causes of laughter and weeping arise from their power, it is established that the intended meaning is: He made laugh and He made weep in this world. There is no connection between this and the joy and sorrow that occur in the Hereafter.

Reflection on the creation of a thing and its opposite contains an indication of the subtle details of God's wisdom, Exalted is He.

In this verse there is the beautiful figure of antithesis (ṭibāq, "muḥsin al-ṭibāq") between laughter and weeping, which are opposites.

Laughter is mentioned before weeping because in it there is a favor (imtinān) through the added emphasis on the power (of God), and by this the verse-ending (fāṣila) is observed.

The position of this sentence in its conjunction is like the position of the sentence ﴿وأنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرى﴾ [An-Najm: 40] under both possibilities. If it is among what is contained in the scrolls of Ibrahim, it is a report of his saying: ﴿وإذا مَرِضْتُ فَهو يَشْفِينِ﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 80].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 44:

Page 144
﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life.﴾ The discourse moves from reflection on God's sole power to produce the causes of joy and sorrow, which are two states that a human soul never fully escapes from one of, to a lesson drawn from His sole power over giving life and causing death, and these are two states that a human being never escapes from one of. For a human being at the beginning of his existence is a dead drop of fluid (nutfah), then a clinging clot (alaqah), then a lump of flesh (mudghah), a dead piece, even though there is in it the substance of life, but the manifestations of life have not yet appeared in it. Then the spirit is breathed into him, and then he passes into life. All of this is by the governance and power of God, exalted is He.

It seems that the intended meaning is the lesson of causing death, because it is the clearer lesson, and as a refutation of their saying, ﴿And nothing destroys us but time﴾. The conjunction of "and gives life" is a completion and a safeguard, as in His saying, ﴿Who created death and life﴾. For this reason He placed "causes death" before "gives life," while observing the rhyme (fasilah), as was mentioned earlier regarding "causes laughter and causes weeping."

The position of the clause is like the position of the clause ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾. If its content is among what the scrolls of Abraham included, then what is related by it is from the speech of Abraham, which God related from him in His saying, ﴿And He who causes me to die and then gives me life﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 81].

The two verbs "causes death" and "gives life" are treated as intransitive, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾ [al-Najm: 43], to manifest the wondrous power over this wise creation, along with an allusion to reasoning about the manner of resurrection and its possibility, which the polytheists deemed impossible; and its evidence lies in the creation of their own selves.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) serves to restrict, in the manner of His saying, ﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾ [al-Najm: 43], in response to the people of ignorance who attribute giving life and causing death to time, and so they said, ﴿And nothing destroys us but time﴾. The meaning here is not the afterlife, because those spoken of do not believe in it, and because it is future while what is spoken of is past.

In this verse there is also the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq), because of the opposition between life and death.

[Page 145]

﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾

Although this verse independently conveys that God creates the two kinds of humankind, male and female, in a wondrous creation from a drop (nutfah) that then develops into the characteristics of its species, and although considering the human species, in its thinking, its capacities and its actions, is enough, this is something the addressees do not ignore. Its mention was therefore only a preface and an introduction to His saying ﴿And that to Him is the final growth﴾ [al-Najm: 47], in the manner of His saying ﴿As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104]. Because this verse is independent in indicating the wondrous formation of human offspring, the clause ﴿And that to Him is the final growth﴾ was joined to it by conjunction. Otherwise, the apparent requirement would have been to say, "Indeed, upon Him is the final growth," without conjunction and with the hamza of inna in the kasra form.

The transition (munasabah) to this clause is that it contains the manner in which life begins.

The pairs (al-zawjayn) here means the male and the female of humankind specifically. This is because the context is consideration of God's wondrous handiwork, and that is most evident in the creation of humans. It is also because people's consideration of their own states is closer and easier for them. And because some pairs of males and females are not formed from a drop but from an egg and other things.

Perhaps the reason for mentioning "the pairs," with "the male and the female" as its substitute, rather than saying "that He created him," meaning the human, from a drop, as He said ﴿So let man look at what he was created from. He was created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 5–6], lies in two matters:

First: the incorporation of the favour within the mention of God's sole creation, by the blessing that He created for every human a spouse, as He said ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves that you may find tranquility in them﴾ [al-Rum: 21].

Second: the indication that both spouses have a share in the drop from which the human is created. Thus the male has a drop and the female has a drop, as in the authentic hadith that "if the man's fluid precedes, the child resembles its father, and if the woman's fluid precedes, the child resembles its mother." By this it becomes clear that each of the male and the female has a drop, although the commonly held view among people before the Qur'an was that the drop (nutfah) is the man's fluid. However, the Qur'an addresses people in terms they understand, and points to what they do not know, until those who reflect understand it.

[Page 146]

It is sufficient for you what has been explained in the hadith mentioned just above.

Nutfah is a form (fu'lah) derived from nataf al-ma', meaning water dripped (qatar). Thus nutfah is a small amount of water, and that from which offspring comes was named nutfah in the sense of mantuf, meaning poured. The man's fluid is poured, and the woman's fluid is also poured, for the woman's fluid comes out together with a tiny ovum which flows with the menstrual blood and settles in a fine sac. When the male makes contact with the female, that ovum descends from the female and mixes with the male's fluid at the bottom of the womb.

The min in ﴿min nutfatin﴾ ("from a drop") is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin), for the creation of the human comes into being and arises through the drop. When the drop is formed and emitted, the creation of the human begins.

Tumna means "is gushed forth," and they also interpreted it as meaning "is ejected."

It was said that tumna means "is shed" (turaq), and they made the name of the valley near Makkah, Mina, derive from this, because the blood of the sacrificial camels is shed there. The lexicographers did not mention among the meanings of mina or amna that it means shedding. This is one of the difficulties of the language.

Then, tumna may be the present tense of amna, with the causative hamza, which fell out in the present tense, so its pattern is tu'fa'alu. It may also be the present tense of mana, like rama, whose pattern is tuf'alu.

The verb in tumna was put into the passive form, because the drop is propelled by a hidden natural force in the body, so the agent of the emission is unknown because it is not apparent.

From al-Akhfash: tumna means tuqaddar ("is decreed"). It is said mana al-mani, meaning the one who decrees decreed. The meaning is: when it is decreed for it, that is, when it is decreed for it to be formed, as in His saying ﴿formed and unformed﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

The restriction with idha tumna ("when it is emitted") is because of what the noun of time contains, indicating the swiftness of creation at the emission of the drop into the woman's womb. For at the meeting of the two drops, the forming of the offspring begins. So this is a hidden indication

[Page 147]

that the ovum, which is the woman's drop, is present in the womb. When the man's drop is emitted upon it, it begins to form, if no obstacle prevents it.

Then, because the verb tumna indicates that the drop is dripped and poured onto something else, since pouring requires something poured upon, it points to the fact that formation occurs only through the pouring of one drop onto another. At the mixing of the two waters, the forming of the offspring takes place. This is the secret of the restriction in His saying idha tumna ("when it is emitted").

In combining "the male and the female" there is the rhetorical embellishment of tibaq (antithesis), because of the semblance of opposition between male and female.

No separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) was used in this clause as it was in the two clauses before it, because there is no call for restriction. No one disputes that God is the creator of creation, and the position of the clause ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ to its end is like the position of the clause ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 47:

﴿And that upon Him is the second creation (al-nash'at al-ukhra)﴾ According to the apparent pattern of the parallel structure, the expected order would have been to place His saying ﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ [al-Najm: 48] before His saying ﴿And that upon Him is the second creation﴾, because of the favour (imtinan) and the display of power (izhar al-iqtidar) contained in His saying ﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ [al-Najm: 48], which are appropriate to His saying ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾ [al-Najm: 43], ﴿And that it is He who causes to die and gives life﴾ [al-Najm: 44], ﴿And that He created the pairs﴾ [al-Najm: 45], etc. This is because the discourse moves from the blessing of creation to the blessing of provision, as in the words of the Exalted, relating about Abraham: ﴿Who created me, and He guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78], ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 79], and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you﴾ [al-Rum: 40]. However, He deviated from that pattern in a manner resembling a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh), so that the mention of His power over the two creations would be joined with the two demonstrations.

Among what resembles this is what al-Wahidi said in explaining the verse of al-Mutanabbi concerning Sayf al-Dawla:

You stood, and there is no doubt in death for one who stands, as if you were in the eyelid of destruction while it sleeps.

Heroes pass by you wounded in defeat, while your face is bright and your smile is cheerful.

When he recited these two verses, Sayf al-Dawla denounced him for matching the second halves of the two verses with their first halves, and said: "You should match the second half of the first with the second, and the second half of the second with the first." Then he said to him: "And you in this are like Imru' al-Qays in his saying:

As if I had not mounted a horse for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,

And I had not poured out the fine wine, nor said to my horses: 'Charge again after retreat!'"

The proper arrangement of the two verses, according to the people of knowledge of poetry, is that the second half of the first should be with the second, and the second with the first, i.e., with the word (li-ladhdhatin) moved from the first half to the second, and the word (wa-lam aqul) moved from the second half to the first, so that the meaning is sound: riding horses is joined with commanding the horses to charge, and pouring wine is joined with embracing the maiden. Abu al-Tayyib replied: "May God prolong the glory of our master. If it is true that the one who corrected this against Imru' al-Qays knows poetry better than he does, then Imru' al-Qays erred and I erred too. Our master knows that the cloth-merchant does not know the garment as the weaver knows it, because the merchant knows its whole and the weaver knows its whole and its details. Imru' al-Qays joined the pleasure of women with the pleasure of riding for hunting, and joined generosity in buying wine for guests with courage in facing enemies. As for me, when I mentioned death at the beginning of the verse, I followed it with mention of destruction (al-radaa) so that it would be homogeneous with it; and since the face of the one who flees cannot be other than frowning, and his eye either weeping, I said: 'your face is bright', to combine the two opposites in meaning." End of quotation.

Had Abu al-Tayyib perceived this verse, he would have cited it to Sayf al-Dawla, and it would have been a stronger proof for him than his interpretation of Imru' al-Qays's poetry.

In the phrase ﴿And that upon Him is the second creation﴾ there is an affirmation of His act of bringing it into being, likened to a right that is obligatory upon the one owing it, in such a way that it does not fail; it is as if it were a binding duty, because God has promised its occurrence in accordance with what divine wisdom requires, since it is evident that nothing can compel Him. The meaning, then, is: God willed the second creation, as in His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy; He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-An'am: 12].

Al-nash'a (creation) is the single instance of al-insha' (bringing into being), i.e., origination and creation.

Al-ukhra (the second/last) is the feminine of al-akhir, i.e., the creation after which there is no other creation. It is the counterpart of the first creation included in His saying: ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ [al-Najm: 45]. This counterpart is the reason for mentioning this second creation.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read al-nash'a on the pattern of fa'la, which is the verbal noun (ism al-masdar) of ansha'a, and not a masdar proper, since the unaugmented nasha'a is not transitive; rather one says anshaa.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it (al-nash'a'a) with an alif after the fatha-marked shin, on the pattern of fa'ala, which is among the patterns of masdars, but it is analogous (maqis) for a verbal noun of a verb whose ain is damma in the past tense, like al-jaza-la and al-fasaha. Therefore al-nash'a with the madd is a samā'ī masdar, like al-ka'aba. Perhaps its lengthening is of the nature of ishba' (vowel-lengthening), like the saying of 'Antara:

yanba'u min dhifra ghadubin jasratin, i.e., yanba'u (it flows).

The fronting of the predicate before the subject of inna (ism inna) is for emphasis on the affirmation which the word (ʿalā) conveys, as an alert to the increase of its affirmation after it has been affirmed by what is in (inna) of emphasis.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 48:

﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices.﴾ The meaning of aghna (enriched) is "made rich," i.e., He gave what brings richness (ghina), and richness (ghina) is the ability to benefit from what one loves to benefit from.

It appears that the meaning of aqna (sufficed/granted property) is the opposite of the meaning of aghna, in keeping with its counterparts which paired opposites: from His saying ﴿He causes to laugh and to weep﴾ [al-Najm: 43], and ﴿He causes to die and to give life﴾ [al-Najm: 44], and ﴿the male and the female﴾ [al-Najm: 45]. For this reason Ibn Zayd, al-Akhfash and Sulayman al-Taymi explained it with the meaning of "satisfied" (arda).

And from Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan: aqna means "made into servants (akhdama)," so it is derived from qinn, which is the slave, or one born into slavery, and this would be an addition beyond enrichment. It was also said: aqna means "gave qunya (possessions/property)," and this is an addition to richness. And from Ibn 'Abbas: aqna means "satisfied (arda)," i.e., satisfied the one whom He enriched with what He gave him, meaning He enriched him until He satisfied him, and this would be an addition in the favour (imtinan).

Page 150
The use of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) is to restrict the attribute of enriching and bestowing sufficiency to Him, exalted is He, to the exclusion of others. This is a restriction based on claim (qasr idda'i), to counter the heedlessness of people regarding thanking God for His blessing, by their attributing provision to its ordinary means, without noticing that God originated the materials of provision and its causes and turned away its obstacles. This is similar to the restriction mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2].
The position of the clause ﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ is like the position of the clause ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾ [al-Najm: 40].

This verse cannot be read as coordinated with the clause ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Najm: 38]. That is because it cannot be among what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim, since al-Shi'ra (Sirius) was not worshipped in the time of Ibrahim or in the time of Musa, peace be upon them both. It is therefore necessary that it be coordinated with the relative particle *mā* in His words ﴿with what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim﴾ [al-Najm: 36], and so on.

Al-Shi'ra: the name of a star among the stars of the constellation al-Jawza' (Orion), exceedingly bright. It is also called *kalb al-Jabbar* (the Dog of the Giant), because the constellation al-Jawza' is also called al-Jabbar by the Arabs. It belongs to the *burūj* (mansions/zodiacal constellations) of spring, meaning those in which the sun's stay falls in the season of spring.

Al-Jawza' was so named because of the intensity of its whiteness in the darkness of the night, likening it to the *shāt al-jawzā'*, which is the black sheep whose middle is white.

The constellation al-Jawza' has many stars, and many of them have particular names. The Arabs imagined the totality of its stars in the form of a man standing with a staff in his hand and a sword at his waist, and therefore they named it al-Jabbar. Sometimes they imagined it in the form of a woman, and they applied to its middle the name *al-minṭaqa* (the belt).

I have not found the reason for its being named al-Shi'ra. It was called the Dog of al-Jabbar because they imagined al-Jabbar as a hunter and al-Shi'ra following him like a dog. Sometimes they called al-Shi'ra the hand of al-Jawza'. It is the brightest star of the constellation al-Jawza'. Al-Shi'ra is described as *al-yamāniyya* (the Yemeni) because it lies in the direction of Yemen. It is described as *al-'Abūr* (with the 'ayn vowelled with a fatḥa), because they claim that it is the spouse of the star Suhayl, and that the two were joined, and that Suhayl descended toward Yemen, so al-Shi'ra followed him and crossed the river of the Milky Way (*al-Majarra*). For this reason it was described as *al-'Abūr* (the one who crosses), in the form *fa'ūl* in the sense of *fā'ila* (feminine active). This is a distinguishing qualification against another star, not of the constellation al-Jawza', which they call al-Shi'ra al-Ghumayṣā' (with a ghayn marked and a ṣād unmarked, in the diminutive form). They mentioned a story for its naming.

Al-Shi'ra is also called *al-mirzam* (on the pattern *minbar*), and it is said *mirzam al-Jawza'*, because its *nawʾ* (rising at dawn with the setting of its counterpart) brings cold rain in the winter season. Thus a noun of instrument was derived for it, *al-mirzam*, which is the intensity of cold. They referred to the north wind as *Umm Mirzam*.

The star al-Shi'ra was worshipped by Khuza'a. The one who established its worship was a man of the chiefs of Khuza'a, who was known by the kunya Abū Kabsha. His name is disputed. In *Tāj al-'Arūs*, on the authority of al-Kalbi, his name is said to be *Jaz'* (with a jīm, a zāy, and a hamza). On the authority of al-Dāraquṭnī, he is *Wajz* (with a wāw, a jīm, and a zāy), son of Ghālib, son of 'Āmir, son of al-Ḥārith, son of Ghubshān, as is stated in the *Tāj*. What is in *Jamharat Ibn Ḥazm* is that al-Ḥārith is Ghubshān al-Khuzā'ī. Some have said that the name of Abū Kabsha is ʿAbd al-Shiʿrā. I do not think it is other than that this is a description that came to dominate him after he took al-Shi'ra as an object of worship for himself and his people. Ibn Ḥazm in *al-Jamhara* did not trouble himself to mention Abū Kabsha.

What the majority hold is that none of the Arabs worshipped al-Shi'ra except Khuza'a. In the *Tafsir* of al-Qurṭubī, on the authority of al-Suddī, Ḥimyar worshipped al-Shi'ra.

Quraysh used to call the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "Abū Kabsha." It was said that this was because he opposed them in the worship of idols. They used to describe him as "the son of Abū Kabsha." It was also said that Abū Kabsha was one of the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ) on his mother's side. They would hint, or obscure to their common people, that he was calling to the worship of al-Shi'ra, intending to cover over the call to the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted. Among that is their saying, when he showed them the splitting of the moon: "Ibn Abī Kabsha has bewitched you." And Abū Sufyān's saying to the group who were with him in the presence of Heraclius: "The affair of the son of Abū Kabsha has become great; he is feared by the king of the Banū al-Aṣfar (the Byzantines)."

Ibn Abī al-Iṣba' said that in this verse there is, of the *badī'* (rhetorical embellishments), the *muḥassin al-tankīt* (the embellishment of pointed allusion), which is that the speaker intends to mention a thing specifically, rather than others that could fill its place, for the sake of a point regarding what is mentioned that favours its coming. So His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that He is the Lord of al-Shi'ra﴾, singled out al-Shi'ra for mention rather than other stars, because among the Arabs there had appeared a man known as Abū Kabsha, who worshipped al-Shi'ra and called a multitude to its worship.

The singling out of al-Shi'ra for mention in this sūra is that the names al-Lāt, al-'Uzzā and Manāt had been mentioned before. They are imaginary objects of worship that have no referents, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are only names you have named﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. He followed this with the refutation of the divinity of the angels, who are among the existent, immaterial, hidden beings. Having followed that with the refutation of the worship of the stars, and since Khuza'a were clients (*ajwār*) of the people of Makkah, when they worshipped al-Shi'ra the worship of stars appeared in the Hijaz. The affirmation that it is created by Allah, the Exalted, is evidence for the refutation of its divinity, because a created thing cannot be a god. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah who created them﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 37]. Along with this, the word al-Shi'ra fits the rhyme endings (*fawāṣil*) of this sūra.

The use of the pronoun of separation (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*) in ﴿He is﴾ (*huwa*) conveys the restriction (*qaṣr*) of the lordship of al-Shi'ra to Allah, the Exalted. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for His being the Lord of what they believed to be among the acts of al-Shi'ra: that is, He is the Lord of those effects and their Determiner, and al-Shi'ra is not the lord of those effects that were attributed to it in their claims. The restriction of al-Shi'ra's being under the Lordship of Allah, the Exalted, is not to the exclusion of anyone else, because they did not believe that al-Shi'ra had a lord other than Allah. This is evident, since among them were those who claimed that al-Shi'ra was a worshipped lady, and among them were those who believed that it acted independently of its own nature.

﴿Wa annahu ahlaka 'Adan al-Ula﴾ [And that He destroyed 'Ad, the first (people)], ﴿wa Thamuda fama abqa﴾ [and Thamud, and He spared none], ﴿wa qawma Nuhin min qablu innahum kanu hum azlama wa atgha﴾ [and the people of Noah before them. Indeed they were the most unjust and the most rebellious].

When the discourse had fully covered what the station of warning requires regarding the falsehood of the people of polytheism, namely their denial of the Prophet ﷺ, their attacks on the Qur'an, their worship of idols, their statements about the angels, their corrupt beliefs concerning the matters of the Hereafter and the Governor of worldly affairs, and since the greater part of their conduct in these errors resembled the conduct of the extinct polytheistic nations, the discourse turned to threatening them, with the fear that what befell those extinct nations would befall them. So it mentioned the most famous of those nations among the Arabs, namely: 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Noah, and the people of Lot.

The placement of this sentence is like the placement of the sentences preceding it, in that it may be additional to what is in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham. It is also possible that it is among what the aforementioned scrolls included, for Abraham came after 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah, and he was contemporary with the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikah) and knew of their destruction.

Because the destruction of these people was well known, the sentence was not joined with the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl).

The description of 'Ad with "al-Ula" (the first) applies on the basis that 'Ad is the name of a tribe, as is evident. The meaning of its being "first" is that it is the first of the Arabs mentioned, and they are the first of the extinct Arabs, and they are the first nation destroyed after the people of Noah.

As for the claim that this 'Ad, when it perished, was succeeded by another nation known as 'Ad Iram or the Second 'Ad, which existed in the time of the Amalekites, it is not correct.

It is possible that "al-Ula" is a descriptive qualifier clarifying meaning, i.e., the earlier 'Ad (al-sabiqah). It has also been said that "al-Ula" is an adjective of greatness, meaning first in the ranks of nations in strength and extent. The introduction to 'Ad was given earlier in Surat al-A'raf.

The mention of Thamud was also given earlier in Surat al-A'raf.

The mention of Noah and his people was given earlier in Surat Al 'Imran and in Surat al-A'raf.

The verse mentioned 'Ad and Thamud before the people of Noah although these were earlier, because 'Ad and Thamud were better known among the Arabs, and their mention was more frequent among them, and their dwellings were in the lands of the Arabs.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿'Adan al-Ula﴾ with the tanwin of 'Adan pronounced clearly and the hamza of "al-Ula" realized fully. Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read (Adan lULa), with the hamza of "al-Ula" dropped after transferring its vowel to the definite article lam, and the nun of the tanwin of "Adan" assimilated into the lam of "lULa". Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', read it with the hamza of "al-Ula" made quiescent after transferring its vowel to the definite article lam (Adan lU'la), in the dialect of those who change the waw arising from the lengthening of the damma into a hamza, as was read (fastawa 'ala su'qihi) [and he stood firm upon his stalks].

The majority read (wa Thamudan) with tanwin, on the basis of applying the name of the tribe's forefather to it. 'Asim and Hamza read it without tanwin, intending the name of the tribe.

The sentence ﴿innahum kanu hum azlama wa atgha﴾ serves as a justification (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿ahlaka 'Adan﴾ to its end. The plural pronoun in ﴿innahum kanu﴾ may refer to the people of Noah, meaning: they were more unjust and more rebellious than 'Ad and Thamud. It may also refer to 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah together, and the meaning would then be: they were more unjust and more rebellious than your people who denied you. In that case it is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, that the messengers before him encountered from their peoples worse than what Muhammad ﷺ encountered. It also contains an allusion that God will spare the community of Muhammad ﷺ and will not destroy it, because He has decreed the entry of its remnant into Islam and then of their descendants.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) in His saying ﴿kanu hum azlama﴾ serves to strengthen the predicate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 53–54:

﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down.﴾ ﴿Then there covered them that which covered.﴾

Al-Mu'tafikah is a descriptive adjective for a omitted noun that is indicated by the derivation of the description, as will come. The estimated phrase is: the overturned towns (al-qura al-mu'tafikah), and they are the four towns of the people of Lot: Sodom (Sadum), Gomorrah (Amurah), Admah (Adimah), and Zeboiim (Sabuyim). In Surat Bara'ah they are described as al-mu'tafikat (the plural form), because the description of a feminine plural may be made plural or be in the singular feminine form. This description has become predominantly attached to them through common usage.

The towns are referred to in the masculine/feminine form according to the inhabitants within them, as a stylistic variation and out of regard for the rhyme endings (al-fawasil).

It is permissible that al-mu'tafikah here be a description of the community (ummah), i.e., the community of Lot, so that it parallels the mention of 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah, as in His saying ﴿And Pharaoh and those before him and the overturned cities brought sin﴾ [al-Haqqah: 9] in Surat al-Haqqah. Al-I'tifak (the overturning) is al-inqilab (the turning over); it is said: "He overturned it, so it overturned." The meaning is: those by which He caused the earth to sink, so He made its uppermost part its lowest, and its mention has already preceded in Surat Bara'ah.

Al-mu'tafikah is in the accusative as the object (maf'ul) of "ahwa", i.e., He dropped it, meaning He made it a plunging thing.

Al-ihwa' is al-isqat (causing to fall): it is said, "ahwahu fa-hawa" (He made him fall, so he fell). The meaning of that is that He lifted them up into the air, then they fell, or He dropped them into the depths of the earth; and this resulted from earthquakes and volcanic eruptions in the earth.

Because al-mu'tafikah has become a proper name, there is no repetition between al-mu'tafikah and "ahwa". The fronting of the object is for emphasis on the lesson of their overturning.

Ghashsha-ha: covered them and struck them from above.
