Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verses 53–54:

﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down.﴾ ﴿Then there covered them that which covered.﴾

Al-Mu'tafikah is a descriptive adjective for a omitted noun that is indicated by the derivation of the description, as will come. The estimated phrase is: the overturned towns (al-qura al-mu'tafikah), and they are the four towns of the people of Lot: Sodom (Sadum), Gomorrah (Amurah), Admah (Adimah), and Zeboiim (Sabuyim). In Surat Bara'ah they are described as al-mu'tafikat (the plural form), because the description of a feminine plural may be made plural or be in the singular feminine form. This description has become predominantly attached to them through common usage.

The towns are referred to in the masculine/feminine form according to the inhabitants within them, as a stylistic variation and out of regard for the rhyme endings (al-fawasil).

It is permissible that al-mu'tafikah here be a description of the community (ummah), i.e., the community of Lot, so that it parallels the mention of 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah, as in His saying ﴿And Pharaoh and those before him and the overturned cities brought sin﴾ [al-Haqqah: 9] in Surat al-Haqqah. Al-I'tifak (the overturning) is al-inqilab (the turning over); it is said: "He overturned it, so it overturned." The meaning is: those by which He caused the earth to sink, so He made its uppermost part its lowest, and its mention has already preceded in Surat Bara'ah.

Al-mu'tafikah is in the accusative as the object (maf'ul) of "ahwa", i.e., He dropped it, meaning He made it a plunging thing.

Al-ihwa' is al-isqat (causing to fall): it is said, "ahwahu fa-hawa" (He made him fall, so he fell). The meaning of that is that He lifted them up into the air, then they fell, or He dropped them into the depths of the earth; and this resulted from earthquakes and volcanic eruptions in the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 55:

﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you doubt?﴾ This is a concluding summation (tafri' fadhlaka) of what was mentioned from the beginning of the surah: of those things that are specific to the Prophet ﷺ, such as His saying ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2] up to His saying ﴿Verily he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]. And of those things that encompass him and others, from His saying ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾ [al-Najm: 43] up to His saying ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49]. For that is a mixture of blessings and their opposites upon mankind, and in their totality is the blessing of teaching the Messenger ﷺ and his community the benefits of reflection upon the handiwork of Allah. Then from His saying ﴿And that He destroyed the 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50] up to here. These are punishments upon the misguided and the wrongdoers in support of the messengers of Allah, and that is a blessing upon all the messengers, and a special blessing upon the Messenger ﷺ, which is his good tidings that Allah will give him victory,

Page 156
So all that was enumerated of blessings upon peoples and punishments upon others is purely blessings for the Messenger ﷺ and for the believers.

"Ayy" is an interrogative noun by which one seeks to distinguish one of several things that share a matter in general by means of a condition specific to it that differentiates some from the rest. Here it is used for equality, as a metonymy for the equivalence of the things enumerated as blessings upon the Messenger ﷺ, since none of these enumerated items falls short of its counterparts in blessing. It is like the saying of Fatima bint al-Khurshub when she was asked: "Which of your sons is the best?" She said: "May they be bereaved of me if I know which of them is the best," meaning: if I knew the answer to the question. And like the saying of al-A'sha:

"With the bravest, one who overcomes by his judgment over time, so from whatever the calamities inflict, I am the most fearless."

The purpose of this interrogation is to remind the Prophet ﷺ of these blessings.
The meaning is that you will never have any doubt about any one of the bounties of your Lord, for they are equal in bestowal. The address in His saying "your Lord" is most apparently to the Prophet ﷺ, and this suits the mention of the bounties and corresponds with the idafa of "Lord" to a singular second-person pronoun in the usage of the Qur'an.

They also permitted that the address in His saying ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord﴾ be to an unspecified person among people, i.e., the deniers, meaning: in view of the fact that nothing among what was enumerated previously is free of a blessing for some people, or in view of the fact that the bounties are not restricted to what has been mentioned, rather the intended meaning is the category of bounties, as in His exalted saying ﴿So which of the bounties of your two Lords will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 13].

"Al-ala'" means blessings. It is a plural whose singular is "ila'" (with a kasra or fatha on the hamza and fatha on the lam, maqsur), and it is said "ilyun" and "alyun," with the lam sukun in both and a final ya' that is vowelled; and it is said "alwun," with a fatha-marked hamza followed by a sukun lam and a final waw that is vowelled, like "dalw."

"Al-tamari" means doubting, and it is a reciprocal form (tafa'ul) from "al-miraya" (doubt). If the address in "your Lord" is to the Prophet ﷺ, then "tatamara" is the intransitive form (mutawi') of "marahu," like "al-tadafu'" is the intransitive form of "dafa'a," as in the saying of al-Munakhkhal:

"So I pushed her, and she was pushed, walking like a sandgrouse towards the pond."

Page 157
The meaning: so which of the bounties of your Lord will they cast doubt upon you about? This is to be considered in light of His exalted saying ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12], i.e., they are not able to cast doubt upon you regarding the occurrence of the bounties of your Lord, which are the blessings of prophethood, and among which is the vision of Jibril at the Lote-Tree of the Boundary. So the discourse is directed to despairing the polytheists of any hope of being spared.
If the address is to an unspecified person, then "tatamara" is a reciprocal form used for intensifying the occurrence of the action, and no simple verb "mara" for disputing is known; rather it is said "amtara," meaning he doubted.

This is an independent resumption (istinaf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) or a concluding summary (fadhlakah, a summing-up) of what came before, depending on the two views about what the demonstrative refers to. If the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an, then because it is present in people's minds, it is treated as a tangible thing present before them and can be pointed to. The speech is then a sudden transition (intiqal iqtidabi) that concludes what precedes it and begins what follows the demonstrative, in the manner of His saying ﴿This is a message for mankind﴾ (Ibrahim 52).

The address is directed to those addressed by most of what is in this surah. For this reason, the speech is described only as a warning (nadhir), without saying "a warner and a bringer of good news," as He said in another verse: ﴿I am only a warner and a bringer of good news for a people who believe﴾ (al-A'raf 188).

Warning is partly explicit, such as His saying ﴿so that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾ (al-Najm 31) and so on, and partly allusive (ta'rid), such as His saying ﴿and that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ (al-Najm 50) and His saying ﴿and that to your Lord is the final end﴾ (al-Najm 42).

If you take the demonstrative to refer to what came before from the beginning of the surah, by interpreting it as "the mentioned" (al-madhkur), or to what has not been informed about by the one who turned away and gave little (al-Najm 33-34), beginning from His saying ﴿Has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Musa?﴾ (al-Najm 36) up to here, according to the two previously mentioned interpretations, then the demonstrative refers to the preceding speech, treating its presence in hearing as its presence in direct witness, so that it can be pointed to.

Nadhir (warner) is literally one who informs of the occurrence of an event harmful to the one informed. Its plural is nudhur, and this is the most well-known form for it. For this reason, Ibn Jurayj and a group of exegetes took the demonstrative to refer to Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is far-fetched.

Nadhir is also used for warning (indhar), which is the informing of the one who informs, in the manner of rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji said: nadhir is used for warning, meaning that it is a verbal noun (ism masdar). From this is His saying ﴿so you will know how My warning was﴾ (al-Mulk 17), meaning My warning. Its plural is also nudhur, and from this is His saying ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ (al-Qamar 23), meaning the warners. Using nadhir for what is speech, namely the Qur'an or some of its verses, is a rational metaphor, or a metaphor according to the view of the majority of lexicographers, while it is a literal usage according to al-Zajjaji's view.

The intended meaning of al-nudhur al-ula is the earlier ones, meaning that the meaning of this speech is among the meanings of the earlier revealed laws, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Among what people have obtained from the words of the earlier prophethood is: if you have no shame, then do what you wish." That is, among the words of the prophets before Islam.

[p. 158]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 53, verses 57–58:

﴿Approaching is the approaching [Hour].﴾ ﴿Beside Allah, there is none to reveal it.﴾

This sentence stands, in relation to the preceding one, in the position of an explanation (bayan) of the warning contained in His saying ﴿This is a warner﴾ [al-Najm: 56].

Its meaning is: "This is a warner of an approaching [event] that has drawn near." The mention of the verb of nearness carries an additional benefit beyond the explanation, namely that the time of what is warned of has come close. Azifa means "qarub" (to draw near), and its literal sense is nearness of place; it was borrowed for nearness of time because people treat time in the manner they treat place, through frequent usage.

Alerting the hearer to the nearness of what is warned of is part of the completeness of the warning, since it urges haste in avoiding what is warned against.

The verb azifat is given a subject from its own root (the cognate accusative construction) for the sake of awe-inspiring effect upon the hearer, so that the mind goes in every possible direction in determining which event it is that has drawn near. It is known that it is among disliked matters, since its mention comes right after the mention of the warning.

The feminine form al-Azifa is understood as referring to the calamity (al-waqi'a) or the event (al-haditha), as one says: "A calamity (nazila) befell him," or "The Inevitable Event (al-waqi'a) occurred," and "A covering (ghashiya) overtook him." The Arabs use the feminine to indicate intensification in the category, and perhaps they took into account that the feminine is the source of multiplicity of the kind.

The definite article in al-Azifa is the definition of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). Within it is an increase of awe, by singling out this genus from among genera, for calling it to mind carries added awe, since it is worthy of reflection regarding the escape from it. Its parallel is the definiteness in "al-hamdu lillah" and their saying: "He sent it al-'iraq" (i.e., in full force).

The statement may allude to an approaching [calamity] in this world of the same kind as that with which 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah were destroyed, which would be their annihilation on the day of Badr; and it may allude to the approaching [event] which is the Resurrection. In either case, nearness is meant as certainty and the impossibility of its being reversed, as in His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1], and His saying: ﴿They see it as far, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6].

The clause ﴿Beside Allah, there is none to reveal it﴾ is either a resumptive explanatory clause (mustanfa'a bayaniyya) or a qualifier of al-Azifa. Kashifa may be a verbal noun on the pattern fa'ila, like al-'afiya and khha'inat al-a'yun, so that the meaning is: "there is no revealing (kashf) of its occurrence." It may also be an active participle with the feminine ending added for intensification, like rawiya, baqi'a and dahiya, meaning: "there is no revealer, strong in revealing, let alone anyone beneath him."

Kashf may mean uncovering in the sense of removal, as in ﴿and He removes the harm (yakshif al-durr)﴾, which is the opposite of what is said of the covering of harm (ghashyat al-durr). The meaning is: no one can remove its threat except Allah. The information that it will occur is given by His saying ﴿there is none to reveal it beside Allah﴾, as a metaphor (kina'ya) for the certainty of its occurrence.

Kashf may also mean removing concealment, i.e., no one who has the capacity to make it clear will declare the time of the Azifa, in the manner of His saying: ﴿None reveals its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. The meaning is that Allah alone knows its time; no one knows it except when He wills to inform one of His messengers or angels of it.

And ﴿min dun Allah﴾ means "other than Allah"; the "min" is extra, for emphasis, and it is connected to the existential predicate implied in the predicate of laysa in His saying "laha" (for it).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 53, verse 59–61:

Page 160
﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾ ﴿And you laugh and do not weep,﴾ ﴿while you are sāmidūn (heedless, proud).﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56] and what is conjoined to it and explained by it, of clarification or description. On this is based an interrogative of denunciation and rebuke.

Al-hadith: speech and report.

The reference is to what was mentioned of warning through the reports of those who denied the messengers. So by al-hadith is meant part of the Qur'an, as in His saying ﴿Do you then deny this discourse?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81].

The sense of 'ajab (wonder) here is astonishment and deeming something far-fetched (al-istib'ad wa al-ihalah), like His saying ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ [Hud: 73], or it is a metonymy for denial (kinayah 'an al-inkar).

Al-dahik: the laughter of mockery.

Al-bukaʾ (weeping) is used for its concomitant, which is fear of Allah, as in the Most High's saying ﴿and they fall down upon their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility﴾ [al-Isra': 109].

From this meaning is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the Muslims when they halted at the rocky tract of Thamud during the expedition of Tabuk: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest there befall you the like of what befell them," i.e., supplicating to Allah that the like of what befell them not befall you, or humbled out of fear that the like of what befell them befall you.

The meaning is: "and you do not fear the evil of the punishment of polytheism, so that you desist from it."

Sāmidūn: from al-sumūd, which is the self-admiration found in a person. It is said: "samada al-ba'ir" when he raised his head in his walking. The state of the arrogant one who turns away from advice and is pleased with what he is in is likened to the state of the camel in its vigour.

It was said that al-sumūd is singing in the dialect of Himyar, and the meaning is: "rejoicing in yourselves, singing songs out of little concern for what you hear of the Qur'an," like His saying ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping﴾ [al-Anfal: 35], according to one of two interpretations.

Page 161
The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for restriction (al-qasr), i.e., this discourse is not worthy that you meet it with laughter, mockery and denial, nor that its hearer should not repent. That is, had you met with your deeds some other speech, you would have had some pretext for your deeds; but as for your meeting this discourse with what you did, there is no excuse for you in it.

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of the denunciation and reproach, which themselves follow from the warning of punishment. On this basis He commands them to prostrate to Allah, because such reproach is meant to sink deep into their hearts and restrain them from the insolence (batar) and the contempt for the one who calls to Allah in which they are engaged. The coherence of the pronouns requires that the address in His words ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ be directed to the polytheists.

Prostration (sujud) may be understood as fear and reverence (khashyah), as in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6]. The meaning is: He commanded them to submit humbly to Allah and to cease denying His Messenger and turning away from the Qur'an, because all of that is contempt for the right of Allah. When they were called to Allah, it was incumbent upon them to reflect and to consider the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger and of the Qur'an.

It is also possible that the intended meaning is the prostration of prayer (sujud al-salah), and the command to it is a metonymy (kinayah) for the command to submit to Islam, for prayer is the emblem (shi'ar) of Islam. Do you not see His words, Exalted is He, ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42], to which they reply, "We were not of those who prayed," meaning: of those whose habit was prayer? A parallel to this is the command to bow (ruku') in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48], in Surat al-Mursalat. Thus both interpretations are admissible.

He joined to this the command to worship Allah, because when they humbly submit to Him as is due, they will worship Him and abandon the worship of idols. The polytheists used to worship the idols by circumambulating them and turning away from the worship of Allah. Do you not see that they went to the Ka'bah and placed the idols in it, so that their circumambulation would be a circumambulation around what was in it of idols?

Or the intended meaning is: worship Him with complete worship, which is the worship that is exclusively devoted to Him, because associating another with Him in worship that belongs to none but Him is like the absence of worship, since association (shirk) is a grave breach of the worship of Allah. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 36].

It is established in the sound reports that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited Surat al-Najm and prostrated at it, that is, at His words ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾. Those Muslims and polytheists who were with him also prostrated, except for an old polytheist, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who took a handful of dust or pebbles and raised it to his forehead, saying, "This is enough for me." It is also related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud used to prostrate at this verse during recitation in prayer.

In Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam (al-Ahkam al-Qur'an), it is mentioned that Ibn 'Umar prostrated at it. In the two Sahihs and the Sunan, from Zayd ibn Thabit, he said: "I recited Surat al-Najm in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not prostrate at it." In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from Abu al-Darda', he said: "I prostrated with the Prophet (ﷺ) eleven prostrations, none of which were from al-mufassal." And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The last practice of the Prophet (ﷺ) was abandoning prostration in al-mufassal." And from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not prostrate in al-mufassal since he migrated to Medina," and Surat al-Najm is from al-mufassal. (Al-mufassal: the later, shorter surahs of the Qur'an, generally beginning from Surat Qaf or Surat al-Hujurat.)

The scholars differed concerning prostration at this verse. Malik said: "The prostration of Surat al-Najm is not among the 'aza'im of the Qur'an," that is, it is not among those at which prostration is prescribed as a Sunnah. This is what he meant by 'aza'im. It does not mean that some prostrations of the Qur'an are 'aza'im and others are not; rather, 'aza'im is a descriptive qualifier (wasf kashif). He did not regard prostration of the Qur'an as occurring in any part of al-mufassal. His companions agreed with him, except Ibn Wahb, who counted it among the 'aza'im of prostration, together with the prostration of Surat al-Inshiqaq and the prostration of Surat al-'Alaq, in agreement with the view of Abu Hanifah. In al-Muntaqa it is stated that this is the view of Ibn Wahb and Ibn Nafi'.

Abu Hanifah said: "It is among the 'aza'im of prostration." Ibn al-'Arabi, in his Ahkam al-Qur'an, attributed the same view to al-Shafi'i, and it is the well-known position in the books of the Shafi'is and the Hanbalis.

The Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated at it, although the command in His words "So prostrate" follows upon the address to the polytheists with reproach, because the Muslims are more entitled to prostrate to Allah, and so that the verbal command might be reinforced by action, so that the polytheists would hasten to it. This served as a reminder to the polytheists to prostrate to Allah, and so they prostrated with the Prophet (ﷺ). Then the prostration at it was abrogated (nusikha) after that, so nothing is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning it after the Hijrah, as well as the report of Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and the practice of the majority of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the people of Medina.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Surat al-Qamar. Among the early generations (al-salaf) it was known as "Surat Iqtarabat al-Sa'ah." In the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite "Qaf" and "Iqtarabat al-Sa'ah" at the two festivals (al-Fitr and al-Adha). By this name al-Bukhari also titled it in the Book of Tafsir.

It is also called "Surat al-Qamar," and al-Tirmidhi translated it by this name. It is called "Surat Iqtarabat," named after its first word.

It is entirely Meccan according to the majority. It is related from Muqatil that he excepted from it His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Or do they say, "We are a victorious host"?﴾ up to His words ﴿and bitter﴾, and he said: it was revealed on the day of Badr. Perhaps this is because the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse on the day of Badr.

It is the thirty-seventh surah in the order of revelation according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Tariq and before Surat Sad.

The number of its verses is fifty-five, by the agreement of those who counted the verses.

The occasion of its revelation is what al-Tirmidhi related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The people of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a sign, and the moon split in Mecca, so there was revealed ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1], up to His words ﴿continuous magic﴾ [al-Qamar: 2].

In al-Wahidi's Asbab al-Nuzul, with its chain to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, he said: The moon split in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), and Quraysh said, "This is the magic of the son of Abu Kabshah; he has bewitched you." So they asked the travellers (al-suffar), and they said, "Yes, we have seen it." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1], and the verses that follow.

[Page 166]

Its revelation was around five years before the Hijrah. In the Sahih, 'A'ishah said: "It was revealed to Muhammad in Mecca, while I was a young girl playing: ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and bitter﴾ [al-Qamar: 46]."

The betrothal to her (i.e., to 'A'ishah by the Prophet, ﷺ) took place in Shawwal three years before the Hijrah, that is, at the end of the fourth year before the Hijrah in Mecca, and 'A'ishah was then six years old. Some exegetes mentioned that the splitting of the moon occurred in the fifth year before the Hijrah. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the interval between the revelation of ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45] and Badr was seven years.

* * *

The recording of the obstinacy of the polytheists in the clear signs, and the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to turn away from their obstinacy.

The warning to them of the approach of the Resurrection and of the hardships they will meet at the time of resurrection.

The reminder to them of what the nations like them suffered of the punishment of this world because they denied the messengers of Allah, and that they will meet the like of what those [nations] met, since they are no better than the disbelievers of the earlier nations.

The warning to them of a battle in which they will be defeated, and then for them is the punishment of the Hereafter, which is more severe.

The informing of them that Allah encompasses their deeds with knowledge, and that He will recompense them with the worst recompense, and will recompense the God-fearing with the best recompense. And the affirmation of resurrection, and the description of some of its circumstances.

Within all of this is the repeated emphasis on the guidance and wisdom of the Qur'an.
